items.title: Nigerians need president with competence, capacity, compassion, commitment – Peter Obi
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA – The presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Peter Obi, has described the kind of leader Nigerians need. Read Also: * Full list: NDC unveils 2027 presidential campaign council * 2027: APC dismisses NDC’s allegation of blocking venues, billboards for campaign According to the former Anambra State governor, the administration of President Bola Tinubu lacked “competence, capacity, compassion and commitment required to address the country’s problems,” insisting that Nigerians needed a president who would be available and responsive. He spoke on Monday night in Abuja at the inauguration of the party’s 118-member National Presidential Campaign Council ahead of January 16, 2027, where certificates of return were presented to NDC candidates. Peter Obi called for a new leadership for Nigeria, saying the country is facing serious challenges under the present administration. Obi said: “Everything is collapsing. Nigerians are looking for new leadership, and I can assure you that we will provide it.” Obi, who is contesting the presidency alongside his running mate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, noted that the country needed a fundamental change in leadership, governance philosophy and public resource management, insisting that Nigerians could no longer afford a government that failed to address their most pressing challenges. NEC meeting The events followed an emergency meeting of the party’s National Executive Committee, NEC, and the inauguration of the newly acquired national secretariat at 393 Etang Obuli Crescent, Jabi, Abuja, which is expected to serve as the party’s administrative headquarters and presidential campaign coordination centre. The NDC intensified its preparations for the 2027 general elections with the inauguration of its newly acquired national secretariat in Jabi, Abuja, the formal inauguration of its National Presidential Campaign Council and the presentation of certificates of return to candidates elected to contest on the party’s platform. The NDC presidential candidate, who warned against electoral malpractice ahead of the 2027 general elections, said the NDC would demand a free, fair and credible election. He urged supporters to go into the country and campaign for the party, just as he warned those who might harass NDC supporters or attempt to manipulate the election that the party would resist such actions. Obi said the party would focus on making Nigeria work and restoring the confidence of Nigerians in their country. Addressing party leaders and supporters at the dinner, Obi painted a grim picture of Nigeria’s socioeconomic conditions, citing poverty, unemployment, insecurity, corruption and the education crisis as evidence of what he described as the failure of the present administration. He argued that the responsibility of government was to solve problems rather than blame political opponents, insisting that an NDC administration would be judged by the improvements it delivered to citizens. The purpose of governance is to solve problems, not to blame people. Kwankwaso and I will not blame anybody. We will create that new Nigeria that is possible,” Obi declared. Economic woes Obi accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of presiding over worsening economic hardship and declining national performance. He argued that the resources available to the government had not translated into meaningful improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians, said Nigerians were increasingly demanding a different kind of leadership, one capable of responding decisively to the country’s challenges and demonstrating accountability in the management of public funds. “From my engagements all over Nigeria, Nigerians are looking for new leadership. And we assure you that we will create that new leadership,” he said. Obi who maintained that the country needed leaders with the competence, capacity, compassion, commitment and physical availability required to address the demands of national governance, argued that the president of Nigeria must be accessible to citizens, responsive to emergencies and willing to visit communities affected by insecurity, rather than remain distant from the realities confronting the population. Declares war on corruption The NDC Presidential Candidate who pledged to launch what he described as an unprecedented battle against corruption, which he identified as a major obstacle to economic development, effective public service delivery and national prosperity, argued that corruption undermined the impact of public expenditure, weakened institutions, discouraged productive investment and deprived citizens of essential services. He maintained that the country’s economic difficulties could not be separated from questions about how public revenues and borrowed funds had been managed, adding, Let me tell you why we must fight corruption head on,” Obi said, questioning the outcomes of the substantial borrowing and expenditure undertaken by the Federal Government in recent years. Obi who also challenged the Tinubu administration to account for the resources it had raised and explain why, despite the availability of public funds, Nigerians continued to experience widespread hardship, said the country needed a system in which public officials could be held accountable for their decisions and public money was demonstrably applied to projects and services that benefited citizens. “We must stop people from stealing public money. We must use public money for public good. And that will be seen, it will be shown,” he said. Obi promised that any public official found culpable of corruption under his proposed administration would be required to answer for their actions, stressing that accountability would be a central principle of his government, just as he called for a fundamental change in the political culture that, in his view, had allowed public officeholders to make promises without being held to measurable standards of performance. The presidential candidate who explained that the NDC would not seek public office merely to explain the difficulties inherited from previous administrations, argued, the party would ask Nigerians to assess its performance through tangible improvements in public services, economic opportunities and the general welfare of citizens. “We don’t want you to hire us to tell you about our problem. It’s only in Nigeria that you hire people and they start reminding you of what happened in the past. No, we don’t want you to hire us. We want you to hire us to improve from today,” he said. Promises emergency measures on security, agriculture Obi identified insecurity as another critical area requiring immediate and sustained government intervention, promising to prioritise security and ensure that communities affected by violence, kidnapping and other criminal activities received decisive attention. He criticised what he described as the failure of political leadership to demonstrate sufficient urgency in responding to security emergencies, insisting that a Nigerian president must be willing to confront crises wherever they occur. Using the kidnapping of large numbers of people as an example, Obi who argued that government officials should not remain detached from operations aimed at rescuing victims and restoring peace to affected communities, said, “If they say there is a problem in Jos, he will go to Jos,” Obi said, outlining his vision of a president who would be physically present and directly engaged when Nigerians faced emergencies. He added that his proposed administration would take the fight against insecurity to affected areas, particularly communities where residents had been displaced or prevented from engaging in farming and other productive activities. Obi also pledged to declare an emergency in agriculture, particularly in the northern part of the country, where he said vast agricultural potential remained underutilised because of insecurity and other constraints. He argued that securing farming communities would enable farmers to return to their fields, increase domestic food production, supply raw materials to industries and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported goods. “We have vast land in the north. When we secure the north, our farmers must go back and produce what we eat and what we use for our industries,” he said. The NDC candidate linked agricultural recovery to the broader objective of reducing hunger, creating employment, stabilising food prices and strengthening the country’s productive base. He said his proposed government would also prioritise education, healthcare and electricity, stressing that the challenges confronting those sectors required coordinated interventions backed by clear performance targets. Education: Obi targets out-of-school children On education, Obi expressed concern over the number of Nigerian children reportedly outside the formal school system, arguing that the country could not achieve sustainable development while millions of young people were denied access to basic education. He pledged to make basic education more accessible and improve its quality, promising that his administration would work to drastically reduce the number of out-of-school children. The former Anambra governor cited his experience in the education sector during his tenure in the state, while also acknowledging the work of other political figures in promoting access to schooling. He maintained that education policy under an NDC administration would be assessed through measurable outcomes rather than announcements and political declarations. For Obi, improving access to education is not merely a social welfare commitment but a necessary investment in human capital, economic productivity and the country’s long-term competitiveness. He argued that children from poor households should not be denied opportunities because of their parents’ economic circumstances or lack of access to influential political connections. The presidential candidate said the NDC wanted to build a society in which ability, opportunity and hard work would matter more than personal connections. “We must create a society where a child of nobody will be somebody without knowing anybody,” he said, calling for an end to what he described as a culture of exclusion and abuse of public trust. 22-year target for primary healthcare in every ward In the health sector, Obi renewed his commitment to strengthening primary healthcare, saying that his proposed administration would work towards establishing a functional primary healthcare centre in every ward in Nigeria within two years. He argued that preventable deaths, particularly those associated with inadequate access to medical facilities and essential services, should no longer be accepted as an inevitable feature of life in the country. The NDC candidate said his government would prioritise accessible healthcare services and ensure that public resources were directed towards improving the conditions under which Nigerians receive medical attention. He also linked improved healthcare delivery to the broader need for effective planning, responsible expenditure and accountability across government institutions. According to Obi, Nigerians should be able to assess progress through visible improvements in healthcare access and service delivery rather than promises that remain unfulfilled after elections. His pledge formed part of a wider commitment to establish measurable benchmarks across key sectors, including education, security, agriculture and electricity. Power sector overhaul, industrial revival Obi also promised an emergency intervention in the electricity sector, arguing that reliable power supply was indispensable to economic growth, industrial expansion and employment creation. He said an NDC administration would prioritise electricity generation, transmission and distribution, insisting that Nigeria could not achieve its economic potential without a substantial improvement in power supply. “We will declare emergency on generation, transmission and distribution,” he said. The former governor argued that unreliable electricity had placed enormous burdens on households, small businesses, manufacturers and service providers, forcing many enterprises to contend with high operating costs and reduced productivity. He promised that improvements in electricity supply would be measurable and visible to Nigerians, rather than remaining an unfulfilled campaign promise. Obi also called for the revival of industries across the country, particularly manufacturing concerns that once provided employment and supported local economic activity. Referring to industrial establishments in Kano, he asked how the country could restore manufacturing capacity and bring abandoned or struggling industries back into productive operation. He argued that Nigeria’s economic recovery required a shift from excessive dependence on consumption and borrowing towards production, enterprise development and the expansion of domestic industrial capacity. The NDC candidate said a functioning industrial sector would help create jobs, increase household incomes, stimulate demand for locally produced goods and strengthen the country’s economic base. He also emphasised the need to support young Nigerians seeking employment and those interested in establishing businesses. NDC targets greater access to credit for SMEs Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) featured prominently in Obi’s economic proposals, with the presidential candidate promising measures to improve access to credit and reduce the burdens facing small businesses. He argued that small businesses were essential to job creation and economic resilience but remained constrained by inadequate financing, high operating costs and multiple taxes and levies. Obi cited figures indicating that Nigeria had more than 40 million SMEs, while claiming that they received less than five per cent of bank lending and credit. He promised that an NDC administration would seek to increase the proportion of credit flowing to small businesses to more than 20 per cent, alongside other measures aimed at helping enterprises expand and create employment. “We will put a mark to it. We will ensure that over 20% of the credits will go to small businesses. We will support them,” he said. He also promised to explore tax holidays and other forms of relief to enable small enterprises to survive their early stages of operation and grow into sustainable businesses. According to him, the current burden of taxation and levies on small businesses discourages entrepreneurship and undermines the ability of young Nigerians to create their own employment opportunities. The NDC candidate argued that a more supportive business environment would help unlock the potential of entrepreneurs, strengthen domestic production and reduce the pressure on government to provide jobs directly for every unemployed person. His proposals, he said, would form part of a wider effort to make the economy more productive and ensure that growth translated into improved living standards. Questions Tinubu over borrowing, public expenditure Obi who also challenged the Federal Government to explain the results achieved with the revenue generated and loans obtained during the Tinubu administration, questioned why the country continued to experience severe economic hardship despite the administration’s claims of improved revenue generation. The presidential candidate referred to the budgets for 2023, 2024 and 2025, arguing that the level of capital expenditure and the reported difficulties facing contractors raised questions about the implementation of government projects. He alleged that capital expenditure had failed to reach 20 per cent across the three budget years, while contractors and suppliers working for government were facing payment difficulties. These claims were central to his argument that corruption and poor management had prevented public expenditure from producing the intended economic benefits. Obi challenged the government to provide Nigerians with a detailed account of the projects executed, the resources expended and the measurable improvements delivered across the country. He also criticised what he described as the failure of the administration to communicate adequately with citizens about its performance. The former governor said his campaign would insist on transparency and accountability, adding that Nigerians deserved to know how public funds were being used and what results they were producing. He maintained that his proposed administration would not ask citizens to accept excuses where measurable improvements were expected. Condemns political harassment, calls for issue-based campaigns Obi also addressed the treatment of NDC supporters and the atmosphere surrounding political mobilisation, warning against the harassment of Nigerians seeking to support the party. He appealed to political actors to maintain civility and recognise that peaceful conduct should not be interpreted as weakness. “Humility and civility is not weakness. It is a virtue. Good behaviour is not weakness. It is a virtue,” he said. He warned against the use of intimidation in political competition, insisting that the 2027 elections should be fought on the strength of ideas, policy proposals and the credibility of candidates. The NDC presidential candidate pledged to campaign across every state of the federation, saying he wanted to engage Nigerians directly and explain the party’s plans for national recovery. He also called for free, fair and credible elections, warning against attempts to manipulate the electoral process. “The revolution that is coming is a revolution of the ballot,” he said, emphasising that the party intended to pursue political change through the democratic process. Obi urged NDC candidates and supporters to take the party’s message to communities across the country, insisting that the presidential contest should provide Nigerians with a clear choice between competing visions for the country. He also promised that his proposed administration would confront the high cost of living and work towards restoring public confidence in government. Pledges presidential accessibility, domestic engagement A recurring theme in Obi’s address was his insistence that the president must be available to respond to national challenges and engage directly with Nigerians. He criticised what he described as excessive foreign travel by President Tinubu and argued that the country needed a leader who would devote sufficient time and attention to domestic problems. Obi said that, if elected, he would prioritise engagement with communities affected by insecurity, poverty and economic dislocation, including states where residents had suffered repeated attacks. He specifically mentioned communities in Plateau, Benue, Zamfara, Sokoto and Borno as places where national leadership should demonstrate solidarity with citizens facing insecurity. The presidential candidate argued that leaders should not retreat from areas experiencing crises but should demonstrate a willingness to confront the challenges and support affected populations. He also pledged to spend his holidays within Nigeria, using the opportunity to engage with communities and understand their circumstances. For Obi, presidential accessibility is closely linked to accountability, responsiveness and the ability to make government institutions work more effectively for citizens. He maintained that Nigerians needed a president who would not only make promises during election campaigns but remain available to monitor implementation and address failures after assuming office Earlier in his remarks, the NDC National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, said the party was formed to strengthen Nigeria’s multi-party democracy and prevent the country from becoming a one-party state. The former Bayelsa State governor who criticised the direction of the APC-led government, particularly on security, corruption and the economy, saying the NDC was offering Nigerians a new political alternative, urged party members and candidates to take the message of a “new Nigeria that is possible” to communities across the country, stressing that the party’s campaign would be based on ideas rather than violence. On his part, the National Chairman of the NDC, Senator Moses Cleopas said the party had demonstrated its capacity by conducting its primaries, selecting candidates and preparing for the 2027 elections within a short period. Cleopas who noted that the party would not make promises it could not fulfill if elected, said that its candidates must be accountable to Nigerians if elected, adding that the certificates of return presented to the candidates contained security codes, warning that anyone attempting to forge or falsely claim a certificate would be committing a criminal offence. “If we fail to bring water for you in two years, if we open our mouth to say, vote for us again, please don’t vote for us,” he said. The chairman maintained that the NDC was determined to establish a political culture in which promises would be treated as obligations and voters would have clear grounds on which to assess elected officials. He urged candidates to approach their campaigns with a sense of responsibility, describing the party’s political mission as an effort to rescue the country from its present difficulties. “We are going for a rescue mission, that the hope of this country is in NDC,” he said. Cleopas also invoked religious imagery to emphasise unity within the party, expressing confidence that the leadership would guide the organisation in the right direction. He called on candidates and supporters to remain committed to the party’s objectives and work to convince Nigerians of the merits of its proposals. The NDC Gubernatorial Candidate in Adamawa State, Senator Aisha Binani expressed appreciation to the party leadership for giving her the opportunity to contest on its platform, assuring that women would mobilise massively for the party. Also speaking, former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, Babachir Lawal whonurged NDC supporters to actively monitor the voting, counting and collation processes during the 2027 elections, advised voters to prepare for a long election day by taking food and essential medication to polling units. Earlier, the NDC Inaugurated its National Campaign Council for the 2027 general elections, with the party’s National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, named chairman and its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, appointed co-Chairman. The Council also includes the party’s National Chairman and vice-presidential candidate, Senator Cleopas Moses Zuwoghe, as vice-chairman, while its National Secretary, Barrister Ikenna Morgan Enekweizu, will serve as co-vice-chairman. Recall that on Sunday, October 25, the NDC released a list containing the full names of its long awaited 2027 campaign council. The Council is populated by 118 members drawn from diverse backgrounds and professions and from across Nigeria’s geopolitical zones. Others details about the Council show that the campaign council is grouped in three categories, namely; National Causes, National Advisory, and National Directorates, that is made up of business tycoons, experienced professionals, tested politicians and others, including its National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson who serves as the Council’s chairman, while its Presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections, Peter Obi, will serve as the Co-Chairman of the Council. NDC National Secretary, is the Council Secretary. The Council will provide strategic leadership, coordinate campaign activities across the country, and drive the mobilisation of Nigerians behind the party’s vision of a new, just, and prosperous Nigeria. The Council is expected to deliver a people-centred and issue-based campaign. NDC called on all party members, supporters, and well-meaning Nigerians to remain united and focused. items.title: Jamestown fishermen threaten demo over delayed operationalisation of cold store
items.description: Some fishermen at the Jamestown Fishing Harbour have threatened to stage a protest if the cold storage facility at the harbour is not operational by December 31, 2026. The fishermen say the delay in putting the facility to use has made it difficult to preserve their catch, resulting in significant post-harvest losses despite increased fish landings. Speaking to Accra-based Citi News, the Chief Fisherman at Jamestown, Nii Armah Wulu, said the facility had remained non-functional since the harbour was opened to the public, leaving fishermen without a crucial means of storing excess fish. He explained that some fishermen had resorted to drying surplus fish along the streets to prevent their catch from going bad. However, the practice was halted following concerns from city authorities, compounding the challenges faced by the fishing community. According to Wulu, repeated assurances from management that steps were being taken to make the facility operational have failed to ease the fishermen’s frustration, as they continue to struggle with preserving their catch. He warned that the fishermen would resort to a symbolic protest by wearing red bands if the facility remained non-operational by the end of the year. “Management continues to assure us that efforts are underway to operationalise the facility. However, frustrated by the prolonged delay, we have resolved to wear red bands in protest if the cold storage facility is not operational by the end of the year,” he said. The fishermen are urging the relevant authorities to expedite work to make the facility functional and help reduce losses associated with the poor preservation of excess fish.

items.title: Oklahoma City Swingman exits on stretcher following gruesome leg injury
items.description: Oklahoma City Thunder guard Jaylen Williams sustained a severe injury during the dying moments of a tightly contested game against the Los Angeles Clippers. The Thunder guard was fouled in a back-and-forth game against the Clippers with less than two minutes to go in the final period. With the Thunder leading late in the fourth quarter, Williams attempted a dunk over two defenders but landed awkwardly, causing a severe injury to his lower leg and ankle. Medical personnel rushed out to cover his leg with towels to hide the severity of the damage. He was then placed in an air cast and stretchered off the court as he gave a reassuring thumbs-up to the fans. An official timeline for the injury has not been released, but the former All-Star is expected to miss the remainder of the season. This is a particularly heartbreaking blow to the 2025 champions, considering Williams missed most of the previous season with lingering wrist and hamstring injuries. The reigning league MVP Gilgeous-Alexander weighed in on losing his co-star during a post-game interview, where he was asked how the team planned to push through the early stages of the season despite the loss. “We have no choice, it’s what we signed up for, and it’s obviously going to be tough without a player like that. “He’s not down forever, he’ll be back better than ever, we just have to hold the floor down until he gets back,” he said. The Thunder went on to win 108-101 at home, recording their first three wins of the season. They aim to maintain their unbeaten streak as they head to Phoenix to face the Suns on October 26.

items.title: Ghana needs TRUST laws to stop the theft of its Children’s Inheritance
items.description: By Agnes Akos Sowu, GIMPA Law School, Greenhill. Imagine this: a twenty-five-year-old in Labadi watches strangers build mansions on land his ancestors preserved. His community’s custodians disposed of it. The proceeds bought cars, funded extravagance and disappeared. He cannot afford a plot. His children will inherit stories about land that should have secured their future. Elsewhere, galamsey swallows a girl’s family farm and poisons their river. Others take the gold. She inherits devastation. This is how a generation robs its descendants. A TRUST is a legal arrangement in which trustees hold and manage property for the benefit of others, called beneficiaries, or for a legally recognised purpose. Trustees must follow binding rules, avoid improper personal gain and account for their stewardship. Breaches can attract court remedies. For Ghana, protection must extend to communities today and generations unborn. Other jurisdictions offer practical lessons. Britain’s National Trust holds designated land under restrictions preventing voluntary sale, preserving it for successive generations while allowing compatible uses. Alaska’s Permanent Fund invests mineral revenues under constitutional protection. Norway channels petroleum income into a sovereign wealth fund, with spending guided by expected investment returns. Exhaustible resources thereby become financial assets capable of supporting future generations. These funds differ from ordinary private TRUSTS, but demonstrate the value of disciplined stewardship. Ghana’s Constitution already recognises fiduciary obligations over communal land and trusteeship over public land and minerals. Those obligations must bite. Lawyers who knowingly help custodians squander communal assets do more than fail their profession: they help one generation disinherit the next. Parliament should enact a Land and Natural Resources Trusteeship Act, requiring community TRUSTS for substantial customary land transactions, protected accounts, independent audits, beneficiary representation and enforceable remedies, consistent with constitutional ownership and revenue arrangements. The law must protect both land that should never be disposed of and proceeds from land lawfully developed. Mining operators must fund community benefits and separately secured rehabilitation obligations. Illegal mining demands prosecution. Publish transactions. Disclose conflicts. Empower beneficiaries to challenge abuse. Remove dishonest trustees and recover misappropriated assets. A TRUST without enforcement is another feeding trough. A chief’s reign ends. A government leaves office. A family head dies. The dispossession survives them.

items.title: At UNGA debate, Pakistan warns against adding more members to Security Council, extending veto privileges
items.description: Pakistan has warned that adding more permanent members to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and extending veto privileges would “deepen existing inequalities, perpetuate historical advantages and increase the risk of Council paralysis”. The counsellor at the Pakistan Mission at UN, Gul Qaiser Sarwani, presented these views at the UN General Assembly during a debate on the use of the veto. He said Pakistan called for “comprehensive, democratic and equitable reform of the UN Security Council” and stressed that the misuse of veto power undermined UNSC’s effectiveness, weakened the credibility of the UN and perpetuated inequalities within the international system. “Strategic rivalries and narrow interests among the Council’s permanent members had repeatedly impeded collective action on international peace and security,” he said, emphasising the “unique legitimacy” of the UNGA, whose universal membership and democratic decision-making enabled it to respond when the UNSC unable to act, including due to the exercise of the veto. The Pakistani delegate opposed the creation of any new permanent seats in an expanded Security Council. On proposals to regulate the use of the veto, he said Pakistan favoured its abolition or, at a minimum, severe restrictions on its use. He emphasised that the veto must not be expanded and reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for General Assembly resolution 76/262, which provides for a UNGA debate following the exercise of a veto to promote greater accountability. Sarwani stressed that any measures to restrain the veto must remain consistent with the UN Charter. He called for a balanced approach combining restrictions on veto use with enhanced representation and a stronger role for elected members of the UNSC, making its decision-making “more democratic and providing an effective check on the exercise of veto power”. The delegate further emphasised that the question of the veto must be addressed alongside the other four interrelated clusters under the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform, as part of a comprehensive reform package. Concluding his remarks, he reiterated “Pakistan’s strong commitment to reform that corrects existing imbalances, strengthens accountability and serves the collective interests of the entire UN membership rather than a select few”. “Reform for all. Privilege for None!” he said. A recent UN report has also warned that the veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council is one of the reasons multilateral mechanisms have been unable to prevent or stop the growing number of state-based conflicts. The resulting paralysis has weakened decision-making processes, prompting the UN secretary general to call for Security Council reforms, including an expansion of its membership to ensure fairer representation, particularly for Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Asia-Pacific region, it says. “All these voices are underrepresented despite bearing much of the burden of peacemaking in an increasingly multipolar world,” the ‘World Social Report 2026’ notes.

items.title: Israelis to decide Netanyahu’s fate in pivotal election today
items.description: A deeply divided Israel will head to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since the October 7, 2023 , attack, with voters delivering their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s rightward drift. Israelis will cast their ballots in the shadow of three years of multi-front regional wars triggered by October 7, with questions over accountability and security central to the campaign. The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by a devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank, and a move towards hard-right religious nationalism. The last polls to be published showed Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, running neck and neck with his main centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot , a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent. Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with more than half a million young people due to cast their ballot for the first time. Surveys show they overwhelmingly identify as centre-right or right-wing. Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad to vote in an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country. “I think this is one of the most important election days in the history of the state of Israel,” Uriel Brandler, a 58-year-old real estate agent, told AFP in Jerusalem the day before the vote. “The country definitely needs a change for the better in every aspect.” Netanyahu, 77, has served as Israel’s prime minister on and off for more than 19 years. The wily political operator focused heavily on his security credentials during his campaign, playing on his relationship with US President Donald Trump and insisting he is the only one who can keep Israelis safe. In the years since October 7, Netanyahu led multiple wars that have seen Israeli forces reduce Gaza to rubble , occupy southern Lebanon and for the first time attack arch-foe Iran with US help. At home, Israelis have faced bombardment from Iran, Hamas, Lebanese group Hezbollah, and Yemen’s Houthi rebels. ‘Not afraid to take action’ Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu “because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons”. Israeli President Isaac Herzog votes at a polling station during Israel’s national election, in Jerusalem, October 27, 2026. — Reuters “He has the full support of the American government,” she said, “and I believe he’s a man who’s not afraid to take action.” Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket. The opposition has scorned the premier for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages. But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at Netanyahu is his failure to take responsibility for the October 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country’s history. Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu’s government has resisted. Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot’s Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left. Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers. Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu have publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 percent of Israel’s population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected. Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament. Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

items.title: Pakistan's last antique restorers give old treasures new life
items.description: Sitting outside his small shop in a warren of alleyways in Rawalpindi, Ahsan Shakeel buffed an antique brass pot to a high shine, pressing it against a mechanised wheel. “We’ve removed all the dents, but it still needs polishing,” the 72-year-old restorer, among the last still practising his craft, told AFP as the spinning buffer sent fine metal dust into the air. Quitting a job as a hotel cook, Shakeel followed in his father’s footsteps to become an antiques restorer, opening his workshop in the Bhabra Bazaar market in densely populated Rawalpindi in 1980. Antique dealer Ahsan Shakeel polishes an artefact outside his shop selling vintage items in Rawalpindi on October 20, 2026. —AFP Today, he is one of the last master restorers preserving antique metalware in Pakistan. Rawalpindi’s roots stretch back to prehistoric human settlements and over centuries the garrison city evolved into a major commercial hub where metalcraft from the Mughal and British colonial periods converged. Moving inside his shop, Shakeel navigated wall-to-wall shelves stacked with centuries-old ewer jugs, samovars for boiling, dishes, jars and teapots, most of which were made of copper or brass. He took down various items and enthusiastically explained to AFP their materials and origins. Antique dealer Shakeel Ahmed works on an artefact at his restoration workshop in Rawalpindi on October 20, 2026. —AFP The vintage items are now increasingly rare in the modern era in which they have been replaced by stainless steel and plastic kitchenware. “I used to travel everywhere, Lahore, Gujranwala, Karachi, back and forth (to purchase antiques),” he said. ‘Life back into the dead’ Shakeel procures the items he restores mostly from scrap yards, ports, or household clearances. “Often, the condition of the items is so bad that no one would buy them,” he said. The shop owner and his colleague Shakeel Ahmed restore the battered items by hammering out dents, re-tinning the interiors over coal fires, and polishing the metal. A badly damaged item could take a few days to fix. Antique dealer Ahsan Shakeel shows an artefact at his shop selling vintage items in Rawalpindi on October 20, 2026. —AFP After restoration, a piece can sell between $100 and $1,000. Shakeel’s customers are mostly collectors or antique enthusiasts, including foreigners. Today, he mostly relies on online platforms and messaging applications to buy and sell antiques. “I don’t have the same health anymore, so I travel less,” he said. Prices for antiques are on the increase but the number of customers has fallen over time, Shakeel said. “The money doesn’t turn over quickly in this business. It’s a very slow trade,” he said. “Customers who still exist, they are not many. They collect these things because they understand these items. Those who don’t understand them would think it’s all useless,” Shakeel added. Antique dealer Shakeel Ahmed works on an artefact at his restoration workshop in Rawalpindi on October 20, 2026. —AFP Ahmed said he enjoyed restoring worn and damaged objects because they carry stories within them from different communities in the past or historical periods. “This is a very old thing,” the 56-year-old man said at his own dimly lit workshop, as he gently used a small hammer to smooth out little dents on a large brass hookah pipe for smoking tobacco. “What we do is like putting life back into the dead,” Ahmed said. Header image: Antique dealer Ahsan Shakeel shows an artefact at his shop selling vintage items in Rawalpindi on October 20, 2026. —AFP

items.title: Ghana faces possible US$50 million default judgment at ECOWAS Court over alleged human rights violations
items.description: The Republic of Ghana faces a possible default judgment at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice in Abuja, Nigeria, following its alleged failure to file a defence in a US$50 million human rights lawsuit brought by Singaporean businessman and investor, Toh You Kang. The businessman, through his lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, Esq., is seeking the cedi equivalent of US$50 million in compensatory damages over alleged violations of his fundamental human rights, including unlawful arrest and detention, denial of fair hearing, infringement of his freedom of movement, and failure by state institutions to protect his rights. The case arises from a series of events involving Mr You Kang, Emmanuel Nii Ashie Moore, the Greater Accra Regional Chairman of the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC), and some officers of the Ghana Police Service. According to the originating application filed before the ECOWAS Court, Mr You Kang travelled to Ghana in May 2025 to resolve outstanding business and financial matters arising from transactions involving Mr Moore. Alleged business transactions and financial dispute Court documents indicate that Mr You Kang, an investor and shareholder in Ghanaian-registered NSG Innovation Limited, was introduced to Mr Moore, who allegedly presented himself as a politically connected businessman capable of facilitating government-related business opportunities in Ghana. The applicant alleges that, relying on these representations, he transferred US$100,000 and later provided an additional US$700,000 in connection with purported contracts to supply electrical cables to the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG). He further claims to have supplied approximately US$1.5 million worth of campaign paraphernalia for the 2024 general elections. According to the application, disagreements subsequently arose over the transactions, prompting Mr You Kang to travel to Ghana in May 2025 to seek a resolution. However, what was intended to be a business engagement allegedly took a dramatic turn when he was taken to a private residence, where armed men led by Mr Emmanuel Ashie Moore allegedly demanded US$3 million from him. Mr You Kang alleges that when he refused, he was assaulted before being handed over to the Ghana Police Service, which subsequently arrested and prosecuted him on a charge of defrauding by false pretences. High Court quashes criminal proceedings The applicant contends that the criminal proceedings instituted against him were unlawful because the alleged transactions forming the basis of the charges allegedly occurred outside Ghana. He maintains that the Dansoman Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the matter. Following his arraignment on May 30, 2025, the Circuit Court remanded him into custody. He subsequently obtained bail from the High Court but remained subject to restrictions on his movement. On September 4, 2025, the High Court granted an application for certiorari, quashing the proceedings before the Circuit Court and prohibiting that court from continuing with the criminal case. The High Court also made consequential orders concerning personal belongings allegedly retained following his arrest. Mr You Kang argues that the circumstances surrounding his arrest, detention and prosecution constituted violations of his rights guaranteed under international human rights instruments. Allegations against Police and Immigration authorities Beyond the criminal proceedings, Mr You Kang accuses certain officers of the Ghana Police Service of failing to act on complaints he lodged against Mr Moore concerning alleged assault, threats and the retention of his personal property. His application references a report by the Police Professional and Standards Bureau (PPSB), which he contends supports aspects of his allegations concerning the conduct of police officers involved in the matter. He further alleges irregularities in the handling of his travel documents upon his arrival at Kotoka International Airport. According to the court documents, his passport was taken by Mr Ashie Moore without him going through arrival formalities by the Immigration Service of Ghana, and it was subsequently discovered that the document did not bear the required Ghanaian entry stamp. The applicant says correspondence from the Ghana Immigration Service acknowledged the irregularity and sought to rectify it at a time he had already undergone the bad treatment of alleged unlawful detention in Ghana. Mr You Kang eventually departed Ghana for Singapore on September 12, 2025. Ghana allegedly fails to defend US$50 million suit Mr You Kang, acting through his lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, Esq., has filed an application requesting the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice to enter judgment by default against the Republic of Ghana. The application, filed in December 2025, is grounded on Ghana’s alleged failure to respond to the substantive human rights action despite having been duly served. According to an affidavit supporting the application, the originating processes were electronically served on November 13, 2025, on the Attorney-General, Deputy Attorney-General, Solicitor-General and other authorised legal officers of the Republic. The applicant maintains that Ghana failed to file a defence within the period prescribed by the Rules of the ECOWAS Court. The lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, relies on Article 35 of the Court’s Rules of Procedure, which provides for the filing of a defence within 30 days of service. He also invokes Article 90(1), which permits an applicant to seek judgment by default where a respondent, having been duly served, fails to lodge a defence within the prescribed period. The application accordingly invites the Court to enter judgment against Ghana and grant the substantive reliefs sought by Mr You Kang. These include declarations that Ghana violated his fundamental human rights and an order directing the Republic to pay the cedi equivalent of US$50 million in compensatory damages, together with legal costs and fees. Press of ECOWAS Court for hearing date Meanwhile, Mr You Kang’s lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, has formally written to the Registry of the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice requesting that a hearing date be fixed for the pending application for judgment by default. In a letter dated April 13, 2026, counsel drew the Court’s attention to an earlier communication from the Registry dated March 6, 2026, indicating that arrangements were being made for the issuance of a hearing notice. The lawyer expressed concern that approximately one month had elapsed without the issuance of the hearing notice or communication of a hearing date. He consequently urged the Registry to expedite the necessary administrative processes to enable the application to be heard without further delay. Responding in a letter dated April 14, 2026, the Chief Registrar of the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, Yaouza Ouro-Sama, acknowledged receipt of counsel’s correspondence. The Chief Registrar explained that the matter was awaiting a directive from the judges and assured counsel that the process was being monitored. He further indicated that the hearing notice would be communicated to the parties once issued. US$50 million claim awaits judicial determination The legal action raises questions concerning Ghana’s obligations under regional and international human rights instruments, particularly regarding the protection of foreign nationals from arbitrary arrest, unlawful detention and alleged abuses by state officials. Mr You Kang maintains that the actions and omissions of Ghanaian state institutions caused him substantial financial losses, reputational damage, emotional distress and interference with his personal liberty and business interests. Through his lawyer, he is asking the ECOWAS Court to hold the Republic of Ghana accountable for the alleged violations and award the compensation sought.

items.title: Tunisie | Organiser l’action publique au service des agriculteurs
items.description: La souveraineté alimentaire figure parmi les enjeux majeurs de la sécurité nationale et de la stabilité économique de la Tunisie. Lors de sa rencontre avec le ministre de l’Agriculture, des Ressources hydrauliques et de la Pêche, le 21 octobre 2026, le président de la République, Kaïs Saïed, a rappelé le potentiel agricole du pays et insisté sur plusieurs priorités : le soutien aux petits agriculteurs, la réussite de la campagne oléicole, la valorisation de l’huile d’olive, la protection des cultures, la disponibilité des intrants et la reconstitution du cheptel. Abdelwaheb Ben Moussa * Ces orientations renvoient à une question fondamentale : comment transformer les ressources, les compétences et les ambitions agricoles de la Tunisie en une capacité durable à satisfaire les besoins alimentaires de sa population ? La réponse ne réside pas uniquement dans l’augmentation de la production. Elle dépend également de l’organisation des filières, de l’accès au financement, du fonctionnement des circuits de commercialisation, de l’efficacité des institutions publiques et de la capacité à convertir les décisions en résultats concrets. La souveraineté alimentaire ne se décrète pas. Elle se construit par une action publique cohérente, des responsabilités clairement définies et une mobilisation efficace des moyens disponibles. Le petit agriculteur, premier maillon à sécuriser Le soutien aux petits agriculteurs constitue l’un des leviers essentiels de cette politique. Ceux-ci doivent pouvoir financer leurs campagnes, acquérir les semences et les engrais nécessaires, entretenir leurs équipements et commercialiser leurs récoltes dans des conditions économiquement viables. Or, les besoins de financement agricole présentent une particularité : les dépenses sont engagées bien avant que les recettes ne soient disponibles. Les échéances de remboursement doivent donc tenir compte des cycles de production, des aléas climatiques et des délais de commercialisation. La création de lignes de financement adaptées, évoquée par le président de la République, ne devrait ainsi pas se limiter à la mobilisation de ressources supplémentaires. Elle appelle un dispositif cohérent associant conditions de crédit accessibles, procédures simplifiées, délais de traitement maîtrisés et modalités de remboursement adaptées aux revenus agricoles. Les banques et les organismes de financement ont, dans ce cadre, un rôle à jouer. Il s’agit de mieux apprécier les besoins réels des exploitations, de distinguer les projets viables selon leurs caractéristiques et de rechercher des mécanismes permettant de financer la campagne sans aggraver les difficultés de trésorerie des producteurs. Cette démarche suppose également une coordination entre les structures agricoles, les organismes de financement et les autorités chargées de la politique économique. Le crédit ne peut, à lui seul, compenser des prix de vente insuffisants, des intrants indisponibles ou des circuits de commercialisation déséquilibrés. Le véritable objectif est de donner au producteur une visibilité suffisante pour investir, produire et renouveler son activité. Huile d’olive et dattes : mieux répartir la valeur créée La campagne oléicole illustre les enjeux de la souveraineté alimentaire, mais aussi ceux de la création de valeur et de la compétitivité extérieure. La production ne constitue que la première étape d’une chaîne qui comprend la collecte, le stockage, la transformation, le conditionnement, le transport et la commercialisation. Les résultats économiques dépendent de la qualité de l’organisation de l’ensemble de ces activités. Le renforcement des capacités de stockage de l’Office national de l’huile doit être envisagé dans cette perspective. Des capacités adaptées peuvent contribuer à mieux organiser la commercialisation et à éviter que les producteurs ne soient contraints de vendre dans des conditions défavorables. Leur efficacité dépend toutefois des volumes effectivement pris en charge, des conditions d’accès au stockage, des ressources financières disponibles et de la stratégie commerciale mise en œuvre. La promotion de l’huile d’olive tunisienne doit également dépasser la seule recherche de débouchés à l’exportation. Le conditionnement local, la différenciation des produits, la traçabilité, la qualité et le développement de marques tunisiennes peuvent contribuer à accroître la valeur ajoutée conservée dans le pays. L’enjeu n’est pas simplement d’exporter davantage, mais de tirer un meilleur rendement économique des ressources mobilisées par les producteurs et les entreprises de la filière. Les mêmes exigences concernent les dattes. Les pratiques de certains intermédiaires évoquées lors de la rencontre présidentielle soulèvent la question de la transparence des transactions et du rapport de force entre producteurs et acheteurs. L’intervention publique doit permettre de mieux connaître les conditions de formation des prix, de prévenir les pratiques abusives et de garantir des transactions transparentes. La fixation d’un prix de référence, si elle est retenue, doit reposer sur des critères explicites et tenir compte des caractéristiques des produits, des coûts de production et des conditions du marché. Elle doit surtout s’accompagner de moyens permettant de rendre le dispositif applicable et d'en évaluer les effets. Sans organisation commerciale efficace, le producteur risque de supporter l’essentiel des contraintes alors qu’une part importante de la valeur est créée en aval de la production. Les intrants agricoles : la disponibilité ne suffit pas Les difficultés liées à la distribution des engrais et à la disponibilité des semences montrent que la performance agricole dépend aussi de la qualité de l’organisation administrative. Un intrant livré après la période optimale d’utilisation peut perdre une partie de son utilité économique. Une procédure de distribution trop longue peut compromettre une campagne, même lorsque les ressources nécessaires existent. La question porte donc autant sur la disponibilité des produits que sur leur répartition, leur acheminement et leur mise à disposition au bon moment. Les services compétents doivent pouvoir anticiper les besoins régionaux, organiser les approvisionnements et suivre les stocks. Les directions régionales de l’agriculture doivent disposer d’une visibilité suffisante sur les ressources disponibles et les difficultés rencontrées sur le terrain. Les écarts entre les besoins exprimés et les quantités distribuées doivent être identifiés et traités avant qu’ils ne compromettent la production. Cette organisation appelle des procédures simples, des responsabilités identifiables et un suivi régulier des délais. Elle nécessite également de prévenir les ruptures d’approvisionnement et de garantir une répartition équitable, fondée sur des critères transparents. La réussite d’une politique agricole se joue souvent dans ces opérations concrètes, moins visibles que les grandes annonces, mais déterminantes pour les producteurs. Recherche scientifique et protection du patrimoine agricole La valorisation des instituts agricoles spécialisés et des travaux universitaires constitue un autre levier à mobiliser. La Tunisie dispose d’une expérience scientifique et technique qui peut contribuer à améliorer les rendements, à adapter les cultures aux contraintes climatiques et à renforcer la prévention des maladies végétales. Mais la production de connaissances ne garantit pas, à elle seule, leur utilisation par les exploitants. Un lien plus direct doit être organisé entre la recherche, les services techniques, les organisations professionnelles et les producteurs. Les résultats scientifiques doivent être traduits en recommandations applicables, expérimentés dans les conditions réelles des exploitations et diffusés selon les besoins des différentes régions. La lutte contre les maladies affectant les oliviers et contre les risques liés à la propagation de la cochenille rouge du palmier, notamment, exige une surveillance continue, un système d’alerte efficace et une intervention coordonnée. La rapidité de détection et la capacité à circonscrire les foyers constituent des éléments essentiels de la protection du patrimoine végétal. Ces missions supposent des moyens adaptés, mais aussi une clarification des responsabilités entre les structures de recherche, les services régionaux et les organismes chargés de la prévention et de l’intervention. L’efficacité doit être appréciée à partir de résultats observables : rapidité de détection, couverture des zones surveillées, délais d’intervention et évolution des foyers identifiés. L’agriculture tunisienne face au défi des petites exploitations Les offices publics : retrouver une capacité d’action mesurable La question du rôle des offices publics mérite une attention particulière. Le président de la République a notamment évoqué la nécessité de reconstituer le cheptel et le recul des fonctions de plusieurs structures spécialisées. Cette situation invite à examiner les missions réellement exercées par les organismes concernés, les moyens dont ils disposent et les résultats qu’ils produisent. Un office public ne peut être évalué uniquement à travers son statut, son organisation administrative ou ses ressources budgétaires. Son utilité dépend de sa capacité à remplir les missions qui lui sont confiées, à répondre aux besoins des producteurs et à contribuer aux objectifs de la politique agricole. Pour les structures intervenant dans la filière oléicole, l’évaluation peut porter sur les capacités de stockage mobilisées, les volumes pris en charge, les conditions de commercialisation et les résultats obtenus. Pour les organismes concernés par l’élevage, elle peut s’appuyer sur l’évolution du cheptel, les services apportés aux éleveurs et les actions menées en faveur du renouvellement des capacités de production. Cette évaluation doit être adaptée aux missions de chaque structure. Elle suppose des objectifs précis, des moyens identifiés, des échéances réalistes et un compte rendu régulier des résultats. La réforme des offices publics ne se réduit donc ni à leur maintien ni à leur réorganisation formelle. Elle doit permettre de déterminer quelles missions doivent être renforcées, quelles fonctions doivent être mieux coordonnées et quelles insuffisances doivent être corrigées. Organiser l’action publique autour de résultats vérifiables La multiplicité des priorités agricoles rend indispensable une coordination efficace entre les institutions. Le ministère de l’Agriculture, les services régionaux, les organismes spécialisés, les établissements de financement et les opérateurs économiques interviennent à différents niveaux d’une même chaîne. Le risque est que chaque structure exécute ses propres activités sans que leur articulation permette d’atteindre les résultats attendus. Pour éviter cet écueil, chaque priorité devrait être accompagnée d’un dispositif de suivi précisant l’organisme responsable, les partenaires concernés, les moyens mobilisés, le calendrier et les indicateurs de résultat. Pour la campagne oléicole, il serait ainsi possible de suivre la disponibilité des capacités de stockage, les quantités collectées et conditionnées localement ainsi que les délais de mise sur le marché. Pour le financement agricole, le suivi pourrait porter sur les délais de traitement des demandes, les crédits effectivement décaissés et leur adéquation avec les cycles de production. Pour les intrants, les indicateurs pourraient mesurer la disponibilité régionale et le respect des périodes d’utilisation. Ces données permettraient de distinguer les moyens engagés, les opérations réalisées et les effets obtenus. Elles faciliteraient également l’identification des retards et l’adoption de mesures correctives. La transparence du suivi ne doit pas être perçue comme une contrainte administrative supplémentaire. Elle constitue un moyen de rendre l’action publique plus lisible, de mieux utiliser les ressources disponibles et de renforcer la confiance des producteurs. De la souveraineté alimentaire à la création de richesse La Tunisie dispose de ressources agricoles, d’un savoir-faire historique et de compétences scientifiques qui constituent des atouts réels. Leur mobilisation exige toutefois de dépasser une approche fragmentée dans laquelle la production, le financement, le stockage, la transformation et la commercialisation sont traités séparément. La souveraineté alimentaire ne signifie pas nécessairement que chaque produit doit être intégralement fourni par la production nationale, quelles que soient les conditions économiques ou climatiques. Elle suppose surtout de renforcer la capacité du pays à sécuriser ses approvisionnements, à développer ses productions compétitives, à réduire ses vulnérabilités et à mieux valoriser ses ressources. Cette ambition doit aussi intégrer les contraintes liées à l’eau, au changement climatique, à la disponibilité des terres et à la rentabilité des exploitations. L’augmentation de la production ne peut être durable que si elle s’appuie sur une gestion raisonnée des ressources naturelles et sur des modèles économiquement viables. Le son de blé subventionné : un système à revoir urgemment Le véritable enjeu est donc de faire converger les politiques agricoles, financières, scientifiques et commerciales autour d’objectifs cohérents. La souveraineté alimentaire devient une réalité lorsque le producteur peut accéder à ses intrants au bon moment, financer sa campagne dans des conditions adaptées, vendre sa récolte dans un cadre transparent et bénéficier d’une chaîne de valeur capable de rémunérer son travail. Elle se consolide lorsque les institutions publiques remplissent effectivement leurs missions et que les résultats peuvent être mesurés. La Tunisie n’a pas seulement besoin de produire davantage. Elle doit mieux organiser les conditions de production, protéger le revenu des agriculteurs et transformer ses ressources agricoles en valeur ajoutée, en emplois et en sécurité économique durable. C’est à cette capacité d’action, davantage qu’à l’ampleur des ambitions affichées, que se mesurera la portée de la souveraineté alimentaire. * Ingénieur informatique et cadre de banque publique. items.title: Full list: NDC unveils 2027 presidential campaign council
items.description: The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has unveiled its National Campaign Council for the 2027 general elections, with the party’s National Leader, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, named chairman and its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, appointed co-chairman. The council also includes the party’s National Chairman and vice-presidential candidate, Senator Cleopas Moses Zuwoghe, as vice-chairman, while its National Secretary, Barrister Ikenna Morgan Enekweizu, will serve as co-vice-chairman. Mallam Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim has been named council secretary and Director-General. The party said the council would coordinate its nationwide campaign and mobilise support for its vision of a “new, just, and prosperous Nigeria”. Below is the full list of members. items.title: Ebola won’t be used as political weapon — NCDC chief
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), Jide Idris, has dismissed suggestions that the Ebola outbreak could be used as a political weapon, insisting that disease concerns would not be exploited for political purposes. Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Monday, Idris said the health sector would not use the outbreak for political ends, adding that any decision on a possible election postponement would depend on the situation. “We in the health sector will not use disease issues as a political weapon,” he said. “When it came, when it came, it came and we were not even sure whether it would be out of the budget…..so no government will use Ebola as a political weapon,” Idris added. On whether the Ebola outbreak could lead to a postponement of the election, the NCDC chief said he hoped such a measure would not become necessary, stressing that the decision was not his to make. “That is not my decision, we hope not because if the thing gets wide enough. As at now there is no need for that,” he said. Explaining Nigeria’s preparedness for the outbreak, Idris said health authorities had been monitoring developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) and anticipating the possibility of the virus reaching Nigeria through international travel and population movement. He said the authorities had tracked the outbreak and committed resources to preparing for the risk of an imported case. “But again you know this Ebola started in DR Congo a couple of months ago and we were tracking and they said we need to track again, that there is a possibility for many reasons that it can get here. A population movement, flight into this country and that side again, we spent funds on it,” Idris said. The NCDC confirmed Nigeria’s first case of the current outbreak in Abuja on October 20, with 53 contacts identified for monitoring. The confirmed patient was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland on Monday, while health authorities continued monitoring contacts. Idris also urged Nigerians to observe regular handwashing, describing the practice as an important measure for reducing the spread of infections. “Most of these infections, handwashing alone can reduce the incidence by almost 40%,” he said. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says handwashing education can reduce diarrhoeal illnesses by 23 to 40 per cent and respiratory illnesses by 16 to 21 per cent. The post Ebola won’t be used as political weapon — NCDC chief appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Israël survivra-t-il à quatre années de plus sous Netanyahu ?
items.description: A l’ouverture des bureaux de vote, ce mardi 27 octobre 2026, une chose doit être claire : quatre années de plus avec le gouvernement actuel constituent une perspective terrifiante pour Israël, estime l’auteur de cet article paru le journal israélien Haaretz du 25 octobre 2026. ** Gideon Levy * Donald Trump a déjà livré le premier mauvais présage : une victoire de Benjamin Netanyahu, a promis le président états-unien, serait immédiatement suivie d’une nouvelle guerre contre l’Iran. Cela devrait suffire à terrifier tous les Israéliens raisonnables et à les empêcher de dormir. Difficile d’imaginer pire désastre qu’un nouveau cycle d’affrontements absurdes avec Téhéran, mais la liste des catastrophes qui se profilent est bien plus longue et bien plus effrayante. La guerre comme seule promesse Que Trump pense pouvoir renforcer le soutien à Netanyahu en promettant un nouveau cycle d’affrontements est profondément déprimant. Dans les dernières années du règne de Netanyahu, la guerre est devenue la seule promesse proposée. C’est le premier dommage irréversible que la droite a infligé à Israël par l’intermédiaire des grands médias : banaliser la promesse de guerre. Quatre années de plus laisseront une empreinte indélébile sur le visage d’Israël. À leur terme, on peut le craindre, la publication de ces mots sera peut-être interdite. Peut-être Haaretz lui-même sera-t-il interdit. Une loi interdisant de critiquer les soldats israéliens est déjà à l’étude. La prison pour «Naza» et Haaretz . Faire de toute remise en question du bien-fondé du sionisme un délit pénal grave est dans les tuyaux. Nous y sommes presque : il ne manque qu’un mandat. Accordez-le-leur et vous verrez. Le coup de force du gouvernement poursuivra sa course, avec davantage de succès cette fois. Une défaite électorale du camp du changement mettra à genoux le mouvement de protestation contre Netanyahu. Tous les bons à rien, les politiciens corrompus et racistes, reviendront au pouvoir, avec une détermination encore plus grande. La victoire ne fera qu’aiguiser leur appétit. Si le fiasco du 7 octobre et les guerres de vengeance sur plusieurs fronts qui ont suivi, toutes aussi absurdes les unes que les autres, ne suffisent pas à faire tomber Netanyahu et son gouvernement de droite, alors rien ne les fera jamais tomber. Si l’incroyable succession d’échecs du gouvernement, des transports à l’éducation en passant par la police, ne permet pas de lui porter le coup fatal qui le ferait s’écrouler, alors nous saurons tous que les Israéliens méritent ce gouvernement et que ce gouvernement mérite les Israéliens. Il est tout simplement impossible de comprendre comment les partis de la coalition au pouvoir parviennent ne serait-ce qu’à franchir le seuil électoral, comment ils peuvent avoir la moindre chance de l’emporter de nouveau. Le changement véritablement spectaculaire viendra de la communauté internationale. Elle en a assez. Jusqu’à présent, c’étaient les organisations de la société civile, presque partout, qui en avaient assez d’Israël. Encore un mandat de ce genre, et les gouvernements les rejoindront et passeront à l’offensive. Israël sera mis à genoux. Tous ceux qui demandent : «À quoi nous sert le reste du monde, de toute façon ?» tomberont des nues. C’est là que réside le grand espoir, bien sûr, mais le prix sera insupportable. Les plans d’action sont déjà dans les tiroirs, prêts à en être sortis. Essayez donc de voir comment réagiront l’Europe et les Etats-Unis après quatre nouvelles années de Netanyahu ; quatre nouvelles années au cours desquelles Israël aura fait un pied de nez arrogant au monde entier et à l’exigence commune qui l’unit : que les Palestiniens obtiennent leurs droits. La vie sous sanctions sera bien plus dure qu’on ne l’imagine ici. Elles toucheront le destin, le portefeuille, la dignité et la liberté de chaque Israélien. Elles seront d’autant plus sévères qu’elles succéderont à des décennies de retenue et de patience dont aucun État voyou n’a jamais bénéficié à un tel degré. Elles déferleront comme un torrent libérateur. Après des années vécues à l’ombre de la Shoah, des sentiments de culpabilité légitimes et de leur exploitation cynique par Israël, des mensonges présentant Israël comme la seule démocratie et comme un pays qui aspire à la paix, la grande explosion surviendra, et elle fera mal. La fin de l’immunité d’Israël Fini David contre Goliath, fini le «peuple élu» , l’unique victime de l’histoire. À la place, un État voyou d’apartheid qui maltraite des milliers de détenus emprisonnés sans procès, perpètre des pogroms contre des innocents, a commis un génocide à Gaza et dont le premier ministre est recherché par la Cour pénale internationale de La Haye. Une victoire de la droite annoncera la fin de l’immunité d’Israël. Cela aussi est une perspective dont on peut se réjouir, mais, là encore, pas du lourd tribut qui sera exigé. Derrière le rideau des isoloirs, face aux bulletins de tous les partis, même avec les convictions de droite les plus ultranationalistes, la soif de vengeance contre les Arabes et le sentiment dominant de supériorité absolue, il est essentiel, cette fois, de se souvenir aussi du prix à payer. Cette fois, ça va nous coûter cher. * Journaliste et écrivain israélien, membre de la direction du quotidien Haaretz ** Le titre e le intertitres sont de la rédaction. L’article Israël survivra-t-il à quatre années de plus sous Netanyahu ? est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Niger : le plus dur commence après les soldats
items.description: CONTRIBUTION . Cinquante-trois ans. C'est le temps qu'il aura fallu pour que des soldats algériens servent de nouveau hors de nos frontières. Le vote du Parlement dimanche 25 octobre est historique, et il a été salué presque à l'unanimité. Mais l'histoire ne retiendra pas le jour où l'ANP est partie. Elle retiendra ce que l'Algérie aura construit grâce à elle. Car ce déploiement n'est pas une fin. C'est un ticket d'entrée. Gazoduc transsaharien : 4 128 kilomètres de vérité Le gazoduc transsaharien relie Warri, au Nigeria, à Hassi R'Mel. Il fait 4 128 kilomètres, dont 841 traversent le Niger. Il doit transporter 20 milliards de mètres cubes par an dans un premier temps, puis 30. Côté algérien, les engins sont à l'œuvre depuis juin, à Aoulef. Côté nigérien, on en est encore aux relevés topographiques. Alger creuse, Niamey mesure. Tout l'enjeu tient dans cet écart. Ce tronçon nigérien est le maillon dont tout dépend. Sans lui, le plus grand projet énergétique du continent reste une belle carte accrochée au mur d'un ministère. Avec lui, l'Algérie devient le pont gazier entre l'Afrique de l'ouest et l'Europe. La sécurité, première monnaie du Sahel Un banquier ne prête pas dans le brouillard. Un investisseur ne signe pas là où personne ne garantit rien. Au Sahel, le premier capital n'est ni le gaz ni le pétrole : c'est la sécurité. C'est précisément ce que l'Algérie apporte en protégeant les installations de Sonatrach, à la demande de Niamey et dans le cadre d'un accord en bonne et due forme. Le message adressé aux bailleurs, aux partenaires comme aux concurrents est limpide : ce corridor a désormais un garant. Et la concurrence existe. Un autre tracé, atlantique, est proposé au Nigeria. Dans cette course, l'avance ne se proclame pas : elle se construit sur le terrain, kilomètre après kilomètre. Le piège à éviter Le Sahel a déjà connu des armées venues protéger des mines et des puits sans que la vie des habitants ne change. On connaît la suite : la méfiance, puis le rejet, puis le départ. L'Algérie n'a pas le droit de reproduire ce scénario. Elle a un avantage que personne ne peut lui disputer : elle n'est pas une puissance lointaine, elle est un voisin. Une frontière commune, une histoire partagée, des familles des deux côtés. Cet avantage n'en restera un que s'il produit vite des résultats visibles. Trois chantiers, tout de suite L’emploi d'abord. Chaque puits foré à Kafra et chaque kilomètre de tube posé au Niger doivent créer des salaires, des formations et des contrats pour des entreprises nigériennes. Une infrastructure dont les populations profitent est une infrastructure qu'elles protègent elles-mêmes. La route ensuite. La transsaharienne, le rail et la fibre optique ne sont pas des projets secondaires. Ce sont eux qui transforment un tuyau en marché. Le gaz traverse le Niger sans s'arrêter ; les camions, eux, s'arrêtent, déchargent et font vivre des villes. Nos PME enfin, et c'est là que tout se jouera. Pour avoir présidé le Conseil national consultatif pour la promotion des PME, je connais à la fois leur potentiel et leurs freins. Sonatrach ouvre la voie, mais un grand groupe ne fait pas à lui seul une présence économique durable. Ce sont les PME qui font vivre un territoire : le BTP, la maintenance, la logistique, l'agroalimentaire, les services. Encore faut-il leur donner les moyens d'y aller. Une PME ne s'aventure pas seule à Agadez ou à Niamey. Il lui faut une assurance-crédit à l'export adaptée au Sahel, des banques qui l'accompagnent de l'autre côté de la frontière, et la possibilité de se regrouper en consortiums pour répondre aux appels d'offres. Il faut aussi que la sous-traitance des grands projets algériens au Niger leur soit réservée en priorité. La diaspora, avec ses compétences, ses capitaux et ses réseaux, peut servir de passerelle naturelle. Elle n'attend qu'un signal. Après les soldats, les bâtisseurs L'ANP a ouvert la porte. Il reste à savoir qui va la franchir. Si ce sont seulement des soldats, ce déploiement restera une parenthèse sécuritaire de plus dans l'histoire du Sahel. Si ce sont aussi des ingénieurs, des entrepreneurs et des investisseurs, il marquera le début d'une ère algérienne en Afrique. La première bataille, celle de la décision, est gagnée. La seconde, celle de l'économie, commence maintenant. *Zaïm Bensaci est ancien président du Conseil national consultatif pour la promotion des PME Important : Les tribunes publiées sur TSA ont pour but de permettre aux lecteurs de participer au débat. Elles ne reflètent pas la position de la rédaction de notre média. L’article Niger : le plus dur commence après les soldats est apparu en premier sur TSA .
