items.title: Jordan strikes militant groups in Syria after church attack
items.description: The Jordanian military said it had struck “terrorist organisations” in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings. It said air force jets had “destroyed several terrorist positions” and killed and wounded “numerous members” of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack . Syrian authorities reported civilian casualties from the raids, with health officials in Daraa province saying six people, including three children and a woman, were killed. Syria’s civil defence agency reported seven deaths in total, six people in Daraa and one in neighbouring Sweida province. On Friday, gunmen killed nine people during a funeral service at the Greek Orthodox St George’s Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate, southern Jordan. Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three per cent of the population. Major General Abdullah al-Maaytah, Jordan’s director of public security, on Monday named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein. The trio, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage, were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces. Members of the Syrian civil defence group known as the White Helmets take part in rescue operations in the aftermath of airstrikes, in Daraa Governorate and As-Suwayda Governorate, Syria, in this handout image released October 27, 2026. — AFP “All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to hospital and are still receiving treatment,” Maaytah told a press conference. ‘We will show them’ One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan’s state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. There were no casualties among the security forces, it added. “This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it,” Maaytah said. Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging. A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said. Jordan’s King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces “chased them to the very end”. “We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote. Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip. “We will show them,” he vowed. Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and “had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack”. “There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties,” he said. Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said “we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan’s security”. Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016 an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead. On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions. Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed. The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday.

items.title: 2027: APC dismisses NDC’s allegation of blocking venues, billboards for campaign
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi, Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has accused the All Progressives Congress, APC, of frustrating its campaign preparations ahead of the 2027 general elections by allegedly denying it access to event venues and billboards. National Publicity Secretary of the NDC, Osa Director, made the allegation during an interview on ARISE TV yesterday, insisting that the party will not be intimidated or prevented from exercising its democratic rights. He said the party had encountered difficulties securing venues despite making payments, adding that its latest venue was the fourth it had attempted to use for its planned activities. “This is the fourth venue we are paying for. We kept this one under wraps until just a few hours ago when we issued the press release, only for us to be called that the political marauders have come and said they are the owners of the land, so we should take back our money,” he said. He added that the party will proceed with its activities, despite the alleged restrictions, insisting that no individual or political party owned the country. “Nigeria belongs to us all. Nobody owns Nigeria. We fought, we used our life and sweat and blood to fight for this democracy we are enjoying today. So who is that person to tell me that I will not have a right to exercise my freedom of speech and freedom of assembly?” he said. The NDC spokesman also alleged that the party had been denied access to billboards but maintained that such restrictions would not prevent it from reaching voters. Speaking on the party’s campaign preparations, Director dismissed suggestions that the NDC was starting late, saying its presidential candidate had already held several town hall meetings across the country. He said the party had held at least four meetings and had nearly completed its engagements across the zones, arguing that its approach differed from campaigns focused on rallies, music and public displays. The party was scheduled to inaugurate its national campaign council, commission its newly acquired national secretariat in Jabi, Abuja, and present certificates of return to its candidates yesterday, the spokesman said the certificates were part of a formal process, adding that the candidates had already been uploaded to the Independent National Electoral Commission’s portal. He also announced that the party would publicly present a statement of its finances and challenged the APC to do the same, saying Nigerians would be surprised by the figures. He defended the party’s anti-defection oath, adding that it was intended to address political defections and what he described as irresponsible politicking. Osa Directoralso said members dissatisfied with the outcome of party primaries had the constitutional right to seek redress in court. Director dismissed allegations that the party’s National Leader, Senator Seriake Dickson, was working for the ruling party, describing the claims as baseless. He further claimed that Peter Obi was the preferred candidate of many Nigerians. And warned that any attempt to restrict the political space could force some democracy advocates to return to the kind of guerrilla journalism practised under military rule. APC rejects NDC’s claim of blocked campaign venues as baseless Reacting to the allegation, the All Progressives Congress, APC, dismissed it, asking whether Nigerians were in kindergarten to be treated to such baseless allegations. The official, who spoke anonymously, said the NDC had not said which state or which ministry was involved. “You want us to be responding to such baseless allegations? The party will not. Are we in kindergarten? Which state? Which ministry denied them the use of facilities?” he queried. items.title: NYSC, UNN disowned ex-minister Uche Nnaji’s certificates, ICPC witness tells court
items.description: An investigator with the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Yakubu Ibrahim, on Monday, told a Federal High Court in Abuja that both the University of Nigeria (UNN) and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) disowned the degree and discharge certificates presented by former Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Uche Nnaji, to the Senate for his ministerial screening in 2023. The witness, Suprintendent of Police, Yakubu Ibrahim, testified as the first prosecution witness in the trial of Nnaji, who is facing a six-count charge marked FHC/ABJ/CR/389/2026, bordering on alleged corruption, fraud, conferring corrupt advantage and providing false information through the alleged presentation of forged university degree and national service certificates. The investigator, who was led in evidence by the prosecution counsel, J. A. Mumini (SAN), said he was part of the ICPC team that investigated two petitions against the defendant. The witness said his team was assigned to investigate the matter after the commission received two separate petitions alleging certificate forgery against Nnaji. He said the Chairman of the Special Task Force directed an investigation, prompting the commission to request relevant documents from the National Assembly, the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), University of Nigeria, Nsukka and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC). He told the court that the team wrote to UNN to authenticate the Bachelor of Science certificate in Microbiology/Biochemistry allegedly submitted by Nnaji to the Senate. According to him, the university responded that it did not issue the certificate to the governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Enugu for the 2027 election. The witness added that the team also contacted the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) over a discharge certificate 15th May 1986, but the NYSC equally disowned it, maintaining that it did not issue any such certificate to the ex-minister. Ibrahim further told the court that UNN supplied the investigators with the defendant’s academic records, including a notice of withdrawal issued over his failure to obtain the required grade in a course. When shown copies of the correspondence between the ICPC and the two institutions, the witness identified the documents, following which the prosecution sought to tender them in evidence. Defence counsel, Wole Olanipekun (SAN), said he would allow the documents to be admitted at that stage but reserve his objection until later. On the steps taken to interview the defendant, Ibrahim said the head of his section issued an invitation, but investigators could not locate his address. He said a copy of the invitation, dated May 5, 2026, was subsequently sent to the defendant’s email address and WhatsApp number. According to the witness, after Nnaji failed to honour the invitation, the ICPC liaised with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to effect his arrest on July 1. He added that the defendant was questioned and made statements dated July 1 and 2. During cross-examination by Olanipekun, the witness admitted that he did not visit UNN during the investigation and did not know the faculty to which the defendant had been admitted. He, however, said members of the investigating team interviewed the university’s Registrar. Asked whether the team established where the alleged certificates were forged, Ibrahim said he did not know. He also said the defendant made no comment on the allegations when questioned by investigators. On whether the team investigated where Nnaji undertook his national service, the witness said it did not because the NYSC had stated that it did not issue the certificate. “The NYSC said the certificate was not issued by it, which was why we didn’t inquire where he served,” he told the court. The witness also confirmed seeing a notice of withdrawal supplied by UNN. When asked to identify it, he identified the document, marked Exhibit C, dated November 7, 1984. He said the university explained in its letter the policy governing the grades required for the award of a certificate saying if one failed four times, the person was not qualified. Ibrahim said Nnaji failed at two stages and did not write the examination at the third stage for medical reasons. “The witness said, “the defendant went ahead to write the supplementary examination for which he did not register.” Ibrahim further testified that UNN confirmed that the BSc certificate in Microbiology and Biochemistry attributed to the defendant was not issued by the university. Olanipekun suggested that a subsequent letter dated March 18, 1985, rescinded the earlier withdrawal notice. Ibrahim agreed, adding that the withdrawal notice related to a course in General Microbiology. The witness also told the court that investigators did not establish the number of years a student studying Microbiology was expected to spend at the university. At the conclusion of cross-examination, the prosecution did not re-examine the witness, following which Justice Joyce Abdulmalik discharged him and adjourned further hearing until November 3. Meanwhile, it is recalled that Nnaji, who resigned as minister following the certificates forgery scandal did not include the controversial degree certificate in his Independent National Electoral Commissioner (INEC) filing ahead of the 2027 election in which he flies the flag of the PDP. The post NYSC, UNN disowned ex-minister Uche Nnaji’s certificates, ICPC witness tells court appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: El Niño: What it means and how Nigerians should prepare
items.description: By Sekinat Osundiji Nigeria may experience increased heat and changing rainfall patterns as a strengthening El Niño event raises concerns about its potential effects on agriculture, water supply, electricity generation and public health. The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said in September 2026 that El Niño was expected to strengthen into a very strong event and persist into early 2027. The Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) has also warned that the phenomenon could affect rainfall patterns, including the length of the rainy season and when it ends. But what is El Niño, how could it affect Nigeria, and what can the country do to prepare? What is El Niño? El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs when surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become warmer than average. This warming affects atmospheric circulation, changing weather patterns around the world. Depending on the region, it can contribute to higher temperatures, reduced or excessive rainfall, and shifts in seasonal conditions. El Niño is part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate pattern that also includes La Niña, its cooler phase, and neutral conditions. According to the WMO, El Niño typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts between nine and 12 months. Although it develops thousands of kilometres from Nigeria, its influence on global atmospheric circulation can affect weather in West Africa. However, its effects vary by location and do not automatically mean drought or extreme heat everywhere. What does El Niño mean for Nigeria? NiMet’s August 2026 seasonal climate update identified the onset of a strong El Niño event and outlined possible implications for rainfall, agriculture, water resources and energy. For August to October 2026, the agency forecast normal to above-normal rainfall across much of northern Nigeria, while parts of the South-West and Cross River State were expected to experience normal to below-normal rainfall. These projections highlight the possibility of different weather outcomes across the country. 1. Higher temperatures and health risks One major concern is the possibility of increased heat. In October 2026, the Climate Impact Lab projected that Nigeria could record an additional 31,400 heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027, compared with an average year. The figure is a model-based estimate of potential excess deaths, not a confirmed death toll or a certainty that those deaths will occur. Extreme heat can cause dehydration, heat exhaustion and potentially fatal heatstroke, particularly among children, older people and outdoor workers. Health authorities should strengthen public awareness campaigns, issue timely heat warnings and prepare health facilities for heat-related emergencies. Residents should drink water regularly, seek shade, limit strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest hours where possible, and check on vulnerable relatives and neighbours. 2. Agriculture and food production Changes in rainfall can disrupt planting schedules and crop development. Prolonged dry spells or an early end to the rainy season could reduce yields, while excessive rainfall may cause flooding and damage farms. NiMet has identified possible agricultural risks in areas expecting below-normal rainfall, including parts of Borno and Yobe. Farmers should monitor updated forecasts, consider early-maturing or drought-tolerant crop varieties where appropriate, and seek advice from agricultural extension officers. In areas expecting heavier rainfall, maintaining drainage channels can help limit damage. Government agencies should also improve farmers’ access to timely weather information and agricultural advice. 3. Water supply and electricity generation Prolonged rainfall deficits can reduce river flows, reservoir levels and groundwater recharge, putting pressure on domestic water supplies and irrigation. Hydropower generation could also be affected if water inflows into dams decline. NiMet has identified reduced water availability and lower reservoir inflows as potential risks, although these do not confirm nationwide water shortages or electricity disruptions. Water authorities should monitor reservoirs and groundwater conditions, identify vulnerable communities and develop contingency plans. Residents can help by repairing leaking taps and avoiding unnecessary water waste. 4. Food prices and household expenses Adverse weather could reduce agricultural output, damage farms and disrupt transportation, placing pressure on food supplies and prices. However, El Niño alone does not mean food prices will rise nationwide. Harvests, storage, transport costs and wider market conditions will also influence prices. The government should monitor food supplies, support farmers in vulnerable areas and strengthen storage and distribution systems to reduce avoidable losses. How should Nigeria prepare? Preparation requires coordinated action by government agencies, state authorities, farmers, health workers, businesses and residents. NiMet should continue issuing updated, location-specific forecasts and ensure warnings reach rural communities and farmers, including those without reliable internet access. Health authorities should educate the public on heat-related illnesses and strengthen emergency responses, particularly for vulnerable populations. Agricultural ministries and extension officers should provide advice on planting dates, crop selection, irrigation and drainage based on current forecasts. Water agencies should monitor dams and reservoirs, reduce distribution losses and plan for communities that may face shortages. Authorities must also prepare for heavy rainfall and flooding rather than focus exclusively on drought. Government agencies, broadcasters and journalists should communicate climate information clearly, distinguish projections from confirmed events and update the public as conditions change. Does El Niño mean Nigeria is heading for disaster? Not necessarily. El Niño increases the likelihood of certain climate-related impacts but does not determine precisely what will happen in every state. The WMO has emphasised that even a very strong event does not produce equally severe effects everywhere. Local weather patterns and other climate drivers can alter its influence. Nigeria’s priority should be to identify areas most vulnerable to heat and rainfall changes and prepare accordingly. Following NiMet’s updates and taking practical precautions can help reduce risks to public health, agriculture, water resources and electricity generation. Ultimately, the challenge is not simply how strong El Niño becomes, but how effectively Nigeria prepares for its potential consequences. items.title: Ifeanyi Okoye emerges 12th President of MAN
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has elected Dr. Ifeanyi Okoye, Chief Executive Officer of Juhel Nigeria Limited, as its 12th President . He succeeds Otunba Francis Meshioye, who completed his four-year tenure at the recently-concluded 54th Annual General Meeting of the association held on 7th October 2026 in Lagos. A statement by Director General of MAN, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, noted that Okoye holds a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy from the University of Ife (now Obafemi Awolowo University) with a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy and an M.Sc. and PhD in Pharmaceutical Technology and Industrial Pharmacy from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, graduating as the best student in his class. He established JUHEL Nigeria Limited in 1987, a wholly indigenous pharmaceutical manufacturing company with headquarters in Enugu, Enugu State, and moved to its permanent site in Emene, Enugu, in 2001 with facilities expanded to include syrups and capsules. In 2010, JUHEL opened a major parenteral manufacturing facility in Awka, Anambra State. Okoye is a Fellow of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria and an alumnus of Harvard Business School in Boston, USA. He attended the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies in Kuru, Plateau State, and was conferred the national honour of Officer of the Order of the Federal Republic (OFR) in 2012. He has served on several committees, including the Ministerial Committee on the Establishment of World-Class Hospitals and Diagnostic Centers from 2013 to 2015; Member of the Governing Council of the Standard Organization of Nigeria (SON) – 2009 to 2022. Before he was elected President, Okoye served MAN in various capacities, including as Chairman of the Enugu, Anambra and Ebonyi States Branches from 1998 to 2005, and as Vice President from 2006 to 2010. items.title: Oil spill in Odidi: Is an end finally in sight?
items.description: •It’s serious, 216 communities affected — Gov Oborevwori •Orders Health Commissioner to deliver medicare •Says Heritage Energy must keep to October deadline By Jimitota Onoyume, Assistant News Editor Has an end finally come for the nearly nine-month crude oil spill in Odidi community, Warri South-West Local Government Area of Delta State? That is the question on the lips of many residents and natives of the area following Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s charge to Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited, HEOSL, to ensure that the company keeps its promise to redress the devastating situation this October. General Manager, Operations Integrity, HEOSL, Nelson Wilbert, had assured that the company was committed to bringing the spill to an end, saying it would work with relevant stakeholders to achieve this. Wilbert spoke when Governor Oborevwori visited the community for an on-the-spot assessment of the situation. What the governor said he saw during the visit while addressing the community appeared far worse than the information he had earlier. After touring the affected areas, Oborevwori expressed shock at the magnitude of the pollution and the economic devastation it had caused. He said he had initially been briefed that about 86 communities were affected, only to discover that the pollution had spread to as many as 216 communities along the coastal lines. “We have come here to see and not just to get report in the office. The thing is spreading. When it started, it was 89 communities. Today from your record, you said 216 communities. We believe there are small small villages that are affected and not captured,“ the governor said. Deeply moved by compassion, he immediately directed his Commissioner for Health, Dr. Joseph Onojaemo to provide urgent medicare for residents of the affected communities, stressing that the intervention of his administration would go beyond the distribution of relief materials, given the severity of the situation. “We have to take this matter seriously. Once you see what is happening, you realise that it is a very big issue. We don’t want our people dying at this time. We cannot afford to lose our focus or waste time. We have to act quickly and decisively,” he said. The governor also directed Heritage to provide medical support services in the affected areas, insisting that residents should be medically examined to determine the possible health implications of prolonged exposure to the pollution. He ordered the Commissioner for Health, Dr. Onojaemo to immediately deploy and coordinate medical teams to the affected communities and ensure that necessary medications are made available. Oborevwori further warned that the state government would not sleep over the matter until the company fulfilled its promise to redress the problem this month, instructing his Commissioner for Environment, Hon. Moses Ogodo, to keep his eyes on development in the area . He also called for genuine dialogue between the company and the host communities to resolve the crisis and prevent further tension. For the governor, the crisis goes beyond compensation. It is about restoring the environment, protecting lives and rescuing the livelihoods of people whose economic activities depend largely on the waters. The spill, which according to community folks started in February from the Trans-Forcados Trunkline, has brought economic activities in Odidi and surrounding communities to a near standstill. Long before the governor’s visit, residents who spoke with Vanguard described the situation as a prolonged nightmare, saying their lives had been turned upside down by the heavily polluted waters. Aquatic life, they said, had been severely affected, while farms had also not been spared. Fishermen, women who trade in fishes and other seafood, and others whose livelihoods depend on the waterways said they had been left with little or nothing to do. “The spill has forced us to remain at home in the last nine months. No river to fish or even periwinkle to pick,” Agnes and others told Vanguard. Residents also alleged that a sexagenarian died few months ago after slipping and hitting her head on hard ground while attempting to walk across a surface stained with the crude oil. “We don’t know what we can call this. Our people are dying; we can’t breathe. Recently, we lost one of our aunties. She fell and couldn’t breathe again because of the pollution. We need the federal, state and local governments to come to our aid,” a woman in the area said. “Life has not been the same in the community in the last nine months,” a woman identified as Timi said. Timi said she eventually relocated to Warri in search of something to do after waiting endlessly for the situation to be resolved. Amid the prolonged crisis, residents have also raised concerns over alleged oil theft around the affected oil facilities. Some community members alleged that oil thieves may have taken advantage of the situation to siphon crude, although they admitted that they could not confirm the allegation or identify those allegedly involved. One resident, who spoke on condition of anonymity, alleged that boats sometimes come to the area to evacuate crude under the guise of protecting the environment. “They come there with boats to remove crude oil; where do they take the crude to?” he asked as he gazed into the air as though the answer was visibly there. The allegation, whether eventually established or not, has added another layer of concern to an already troubling situation and heightened calls for greater transparency around activities at the affected facilities. For the people of Odidi and the other affected communities, however, the immediate concern is simple: they want the oil to stop flowing and their lives to begin again. They say Heritage’s promise to end the spill will only become something to celebrate when the pollution is actually stopped, the affected environment is properly remediated and efforts are made to restore the aquatic life on which thousands depend. Now, with October fast coming to an end and the governor demanding action, the question is no longer merely when the promise will be fulfilled. Will October finally bring an end to Odidi’s agonising oil-spill nightmare, or will the month slide away with the promise being yet another chapter in a crisis that has already lasted almost nine months? items.title: Okpebholo’s CNG buses: Road users express concern over refuelling
items.description: • We’ve procured mobile kits for gas filling — Commissioner By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY – Residents of Edo State have been asking if the 50 new CNG buses launched in Benin City, Edo State recently will ease transportation costs and movement in the state; time will tell. SINCE 2011 when the government of Comrade Adams Oshiomhole established the Edo City Transport Service from the then moribund Edo Municipal Transport Service established by the government of Chief John Odigie-Oyegun, the people of the state heaved a sigh of relief from the stress of intra state transport services. The ECTS buses are branded Comrade Bus and as a matter of policy, the prices are cheaper than the regular commercial vehicles and they are deployed across popular routes in the state capital and some other local government areas. Every student in uniform and those with verifiable identity cards did not pay a fare, they had free rides throughout the period of Oshiomhole’s administration. Oshiomhole started the scheme with about 75 buses painted in green. The administration of Godwin Obaseki boosted it in 2017 with 100 additional buses painted oxblood red. But by the end of Obaseki’s tenure, most of the buses he added were nowhere in the state and that put more pressure on the original ones acquired by Oshiomhole. Till date, the buses acquired by Oshiomole are still in operation but fewer in number and devoid of the luxury of air conditioners and digital payment structure. The Comrade Buses are overcrowded and grossly insufficient to meet the peoples’ demand. The ECTS terminals within the city are always crowded with passengers waiting for the cheap transport fare. The limited availability of the buses forced many to revert to the commercial buses. Governor Monday Okpebholo acquired another set of 50 new CNG buses and they were launched by Nigeria’s First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu on Thursday. The development brought a feeling of renewed hope in the government’s transport scheme. At the Garrick Memorial College ground, venue of the commissioning which was graced by not less than 15 First Ladies from states across Nigeria, Governor Usman Ododo of Kogi, the Managing Director of Zenith Bank, Dr. Adaora Umeoji, Minister of Regional Development, Hon. Abubakar Momoh, Sen. Oshiomhole among others, Mrs Oluremi Tinubu commended the initiative of Governor Okpebholo saying that it would help civil servants, parents taking their children to and from schools, students, market women and other low income earners to move easily around the state. She said the initiative was key to her husband’s reforms which is to make Nigeria patronise alternative sources of energy for mobility like gas and solar-powered vehicles. She said: “I am glad to be in Edo State today after quite a long time for the commissioning of 50 compressed natural gas buses for the benefit of the people of this state. “We are not merely commissioning buses; we are commissioning opportunities, mobility and home because behind every bus is a human story, there is a student who needs to get to school, there is a trader who needs to get to the market. There is a mother who needs to take her children to school and return to her business. There is a young person travelling to work. There is an artisan moving to a job site. There is a civil servant going to work. “That is why today’s event is a story of renewed hope. When transportation becomes more affordable and accessible, economic opportunities become a reality. Nigeria is blessed with abundant natural gas resources and the Federal Government under the renewed hope agenda of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR has continued to support the development of a compressed natural gas ecosystem towards providing more affordable transportation for Nigerians. “It is not only gas, you can see that electric cars have started coming up as well and we have this sunshine for solar energy and so we are just getting there.” An elated Governor Okpebholo commended President Bola Tinubu whose reforms he said had made more resources available for development and good governance. “We understand the daily challenges faced by our workers, traders, students and families. High cost of transportation puts pressure on household income, business activities and the overall cost of living. “These buses are more than just vehicles; they are a practical way to reduce transport costs, ease the burden on families and improve the daily lives of Edo people. “Mr.President’s economic reforms have increased our revenues which enables us to deliver more dividends of democracy to our people.” Several market women, students and civil servants praised the initiative and lauded the government. The buses are expected to be deployed to ease the pains of the increase in transport fare as a result of the removal of the subsidy on petrol. But commuters expressed fears that the fleet may plunge into the challenge of refueling because of the limited number of gas stations in the state capital which are already overwhelmed with the number of vehicles that throng them to get gas. But the Commissioner for Transportation, Saturday Uwuilekhue told NDV that the government has a structure in place for refuelling the buses, adding that they have been deployed into the fleet of the ECTS and have started operations.“They are already plying the roads, they are part of the ECTS and they will be running across the state. We have acquired our CNG mobile refuelling units to enhance efficiency,“ he said. The post Okpebholo’s CNG buses: Road users express concern over refuelling appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG launches trade intelligence tools to boost exports, investment
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Federal Government has launched new trade intelligence tools to help Nigerian businesses access international markets, attract productive investments and strengthen local industries’ competitiveness as part of efforts to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030. Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, who unveiled the initiative in Abuja, said the tools would provide exporters and investors with reliable market information to guide business decisions, navigate trade requirements and translate economic reforms into industrial growth and job creation. Oduwole said Nigeria had recorded significant progress in capital inflows and non-oil exports, but stressed the need to convert the gains into productive investments, completed export transactions and stronger domestic industries. She disclosed that capital importation rose from about $3.9 billion in 2023 to more than $23 billion in 2025, while non-oil exports reached a record N12.36 trillion, with Nigerian products gaining access to more than 120 countries. The minister also said intra-African trade grew by 21 per cent in 2025, describing the development as an opportunity for Nigeria to expand its participation in regional and global markets. However, she acknowledged that businesses continued to face high production costs, limited access to finance, logistics constraints and complex trade procedures. According to her, the new tools would help exporters identify promising markets, understand applicable tariffs and entry requirements, and obtain credible information before shipping their products. Oduwole identified the forthcoming CANEX Weekend 2026 and the Intra-African Trade Fair 2027, both strategic platforms for promoting Nigerian products and connecting businesses with international buyers and investors, as key opportunities to expand trade. She announced that the ministry planned to formally launch its Trade Portal at CANEX Weekend, scheduled for November 5 to 8, 2026. The portal is expected to provide businesses with market intelligence and help convert trade contacts into actual commercial transactions. Meanwhile, President of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture, NACCIMA, Jani Ibrahim, called for increased private-sector investment in value-added exports, competitive manufacturing and priority export value chains. Ibrahim said such investments would improve the global competitiveness of Nigerian products, increase domestic value addition and create more jobs. He stressed the importance of strengthening local industries to enable Nigeria to take greater advantage of emerging opportunities in regional and international markets. items.title: Whither terrorism
items.description: THE future of Khyber Pakhtun­khwa remains unclear, whether it’s as a single entity or as a democratic one. PTI, we are told, has been made PNG — once again. And the south of KP is reportedly being carved out rapidly to be a new province or to simply reverse the amendment that made the former Fata part of KP. No one is really sure what the coming days hold. Amid this confusion, a newly appointed member of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) for the special emergency-hit districts of the south has created another storm in a teacup. In a video statement he spoke of reaching out to the Afghan Taliban to bring peace to Pakistan. Considering that this preference for dialogue over conflict with the fitna-across-the-border ostensibly has been the reason the PTI government was sent home, a similar message of love from the new advisory council just wasn’t cricket. But before we could get our breath back at this audacity, the new spokesman of the region, Mehmood Jan Babar, added to the mess by not denying the idea altogether. Eventually Samar Bilour, who represents the Peshawar-led advisory council, had to enter the fray to diss the notion of talks. As an aside, we now have a Peshawar council and a Southern council. Be that as it may, the point is these statements have simply added to the confusion surrounding the province. And terrorism, despite the frequency of the attacks and the statements of the government, has taken a backseat. The focus is more on what the grand plan for KP is. Is it simply to close the doors on PTI? Is it to conduct an experiment on the efficacy of newer, smaller provinces? Or is it simply to reverse the Fata merger? Or perhaps it was to give the governor the chance to clear encroachments, a favourite problem for most non-elected officials these days. As the Urdu saying goes, there are as many rumours as there are mouths. We appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period. But none of these rumours seem to be highlighting the basic issue — how to address the decades-old problem of militancy in these regions. Other than vague promises of fighting the problem, there is little that has been shared with the people to explain what the new government is doing or planning to do. And this is where the problem lies. Militancy is going from bad to worse. The intensity of the attacks is worrying and impacts the entire country, especially one looking for more foreign investment. But while the state is clear on its decision to fight its way to victory, it doesn’t seem to have a clear strategy or path for this — or so it appears to those on the outside. Any strategy to succeed must take into account the current environment. However, we appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period when the TTP was controlling large swathes of land in what is now former Fata. In order to flush the Taliban out, military operations were conducted after the ordinary residents were persuaded to leave their homes and villages before the clearing out was done. And once the area/s were cleared, the displaced people were allowed to return to their homes and businesses. However, nearly two decades later, the TTP is no longer controlling areas; it seems to appear only to conduct attacks or block roads, or carry out other activities and then melt away. And yet, it seems, our strategy remains the same — of wanting to clear out areas, be it at the level of villages and so on. But if the TTP is not controlling these areas and the plan is to clear out the residents before launching operations, surely the TTP will also vacate the areas along with the residents and simply return later. How is this effective? And this is all the more difficult now because 20 years earlier, the TTP escaped to an Afghanistan run by a hostile government, which is no longer the case. But these questions are really not being discussed. The intelligence-based operations (IBOs) are also offered as an alternative. Though once again, there is little clarity on how effective these are; they only become public when they lead to deaths of troops, which is tragic. But once again, there is little information available on why there is even one fatality during an IBO. And if they are effective, then why has the problem simply grown? The second problem with this strategy is the public sentiment, which is against military operations because of the displacement and suffering that comes in the wake of this. But more than that, the displacements were not accompanied by the compensation the people had been promised — for the damage to their property and business. This has been a major reason for their reluctance to support operations this time around. And yet, this also does not seem to have led to any kind of brainstorming about what to do differently. More worrying still is the distrust or alienation of the people in general from the state as well as the TTP. In many anecdotal accounts, it is suggested the local residents of the affected areas see the activities of the TTP and the state as alienating. These gaps with the state, ideally, should be bridged before operations are launched. It is rather obvious that kinetic operations cannot succeed without the people’s support. And yet the state seems to be doing little to earn this support or trust. And along with all this comes the larger issue of why the kinetic operations, whenever they have succeeded, are not followed by a successful handover to strong functioning civilian institutions which can then govern effectively. In other words, the build-and-transfer part has eluded us for decades. Indeed, the reduction of the debate over terrorism to a simple one of using force or not is a very one-dimensional one. The problem requires a lot more depth and nuance than is realised. The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

items.title: Ogo-Eze schools in ruins: Pupils, students sit on floor, receive lectures amidst reptiles
items.description: •No teachers for Maths, other core subjects — Gougou •Declare emergency in schools — Group By Chancel Bomadi Sunday BOMADI — For pupils of Ogo-Eze Primary School and students of Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School in Delta State, it’s a sad story. They learn on bare floors in their classrooms, with crawling insects and reptiles all over. There is the case of severe shortage of teachers. The two schools, located in Ogodobiri and Ezebiri communities in Bomadi Local Government Area, present a disturbing picture of neglect that community leaders say requires urgent government intervention. Ogodobiri and Ezebiri are sister communities situated along the banks of the Forcados River in the creeks of Delta State. Collectively known as Ogo-Eze Community, they share the two schools, making their deteriorating condition a concern for families across both communities. The Chairman of Ogodobiri Community, Mr Koboye Benin, called on the state government to urgently provide desks for pupils, students and teachers, renovate the school buildings and deploy more teachers. He lamented the shortage of furniture and teaching personnel, warning that the deficiencies were undermining the children’s education. He appealed to the government to provide the basic facilities and manpower required to restore effective teaching and learning. The Amanana-Owei of Ogo-Eze Community, Archbishop Stephen Overy, also expressed concern over the condition of the classroom blocks, describing the environment in which pupils, students and teachers operate as harsh and potentially dangerous to their health. “Both the primary and secondary school buildings are long overdue for renovation, and I appeal to the government to come to the aid of our children. We are suffering, and action must be taken without further delay,” he said. The community leader’s appeal reflects growing anxiety among residents who fear that continued neglect could further compromise the quality of education available to their children. The situation at Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School is particularly troubling, according to its Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) Chairman, Pastor Jeremiah Gougou. He said students were forced to sit on bare floor or squeeze onto the few available desks during lessons, leaving them exposed to the discomfort of rain and sunshine where classrooms offer inadequate protection. “Our students sit on the floor to learn, while others occupy the dilapidated desks during lectures, which is unfortunate,” he said. Gougou also decried the shortage of teachers, particularly in core subjects such as Mathematics, English Language, Chemistry and Biology. “There are no teachers available to teach our students because we lack teachers in Mathematics, English Language, Chemistry and Biology. One teacher is burdened with the task of moving from one subject to another. The total number of teachers in the school is no more than three or four,” he said. The shortage, he explained, places an enormous burden on the few available teachers and raises concerns about the students’ ability to receive adequate instruction across the curriculum. Political leaders demand a state of emergency The Bomadi Political Leaders Forum (BPLF) has joined the call for urgent intervention, urging Governor Sheriff Oborevwori to take decisive action to rescue the two schools. The forum called for a state of emergency to be declared on the schools, citing their dilapidated infrastructure, inadequate furniture, shortage of teachers and unsafe learning conditions. Its Chairman, Comrade Felix Okpe, said the forum’s visit to the schools had reinforced the need for immediate government action. Speaking to NDV over the weekend, Okpe said the condition of the schools was unacceptable and called for a comprehensive rehabilitation programme to restore a safe and functional learning environment. “We are conveying this message to the Governor of Delta State . There is urgent need for renovation of the schools. It is evident that our people are dissatisfied with their children having to learn in such dilapidated classrooms,” he said. Okpe expressed particular concern over the condition of Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School, which he said was established in 1978 but now faced severe infrastructure and staffing challenges. He reiterated that the school lacked teachers for core subjects . “We did not expect our children sitting on a floor with reptiles and ants while attending their lessons; this is an aberration,” he said. Beyond the need to renovate the classroom blocks and recruit more teachers, Okpe said the secondary school also lacked computers and other office equipment expected of a commercial institution. He warned that the deteriorating condition of the schools was already affecting enrolment, with many parents reportedly transferring their children to schools outside the Ogo-Eze community. The forum appealed to the governor to intervene without delay and urged the community’s representatives in the National Assembly and Delta State House of Assembly to support efforts to rehabilitate the schools. Governor Oborevwori recently spoke of move by his administration to commence rehabilitation of delapidated schools in the state. Our reporter could not confirm if Ogo-Eze Primary School and Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School were included in the proposed rehabilitation programme. items.title: BoI secures €2.22bn, N250bn funding for Nigerian industries
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Bank of Industry (BoI) has secured more than €2.22 billion and N250 billion in new funding through major financing transactions concluded between 2024 and 2026, as the development finance institution intensifies efforts to bridge Nigeria’s industrial financing gap. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of BoI, Dr. Olasupo Olusi, disclosed this at a media roundtable, highlighting the bank’s capital mobilisation drive as a key pillar of its 2025–2027 corporate strategy. The transactions include a €1.879 billion syndicated facility secured in 2024, €210 million raised from international development partners in 2025, and a N250 billion development bond issued in 2026, which was oversubscribed. The bank also secured €85 million from the European Investment Bank (EIB) in 2026 to support agriculture, alongside another €50 million facility from the European lender for healthcare manufacturing. Olusi said the funding transactions reflected growing investor confidence in the bank’s governance, financing pipeline and development impact. “Nigerian businesses need long-term, affordable capital, and the commercial banking system cannot provide enough of it. Filling that gap is our job,” he said. He added: “Investors have placed this money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline and our results.” The €1.879 billion syndicated facility, concluded in 2024, was subsequently recognised as Syndicated Loan Deal of the Year, while the oversubscription of the N250 billion development bond underscored investor appetite for the bank’s industrial financing activities. The EIB facilities are expected to strengthen financing for domestic agricultural production and healthcare manufacturing, supporting efforts to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported food and medicines. Olusi said the capital-raising drive was central to the bank’s ambition to spearhead sustainable and inclusive industrial development, with particular attention to manufacturing, infrastructure and underserved businesses. Under its 2025–2027 corporate strategy, BoI aims to double its loan book, disbursements and development impact instruments within three years. The bank has prioritised 15 sectors grouped under agro-manufacturing, other manufacturing, infrastructure, extractive industries and services. Olusi said 80 per cent of its large-enterprise lending now goes to manufacturing and infrastructure, reflecting their capacity to generate jobs and economic output. The bank’s financing activities have also expanded significantly. In 2025, it disbursed N644.9 billion, representing a 26 per cent increase over the N510.9 billion recorded in 2024. The funds reached 12,501 businesses and created or supported 1.68 million jobs. Of the 2025 disbursements, N120.9 billion went to women-owned businesses, while micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) received 41 per cent of total funding, above the bank’s 35 per cent target. Beyond funds raised from investors and development partners, BoI is implementing a N200 billion Federal Government intervention package comprising a N50 billion Presidential Conditional Grant Scheme, a N75 billion MSME Intervention Fund and a N75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund. Olusi said more than 95 per cent of the intervention had been delivered, reaching 957,400 grant beneficiaries, 9,000 MSMEs and 104 large manufacturers. The bank also disbursed N213 billion to agro-allied businesses and linked 47,508 smallholder farmers to processors. Through its Rural Area Programme on Investment for Development (RAPID), it disbursed N6.5 billion to 880 rural enterprises across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, supporting more than 8,000 jobs. Looking ahead, Olusi said BoI would deploy the new EIB facilities to agriculture and local healthcare manufacturing, expand financing for information and communications technology businesses through the iDICE programme, and work with the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment on a National Industrial Finance Compact to mobilise additional long-term capital. “Our mission is simple: finance what Nigeria makes, and create jobs for Nigerians,” he said. items.title: Russie-Afrique : Moscou défend un modèle de coopération fondé sur l’indépendance des États
items.description: En prélude au Sommet Russie-Afrique, auquel prendra part le Premier ministre burkinabè, Rimtalba Jean-Emmanuel Ouédraogo, le directeur adjoint de l’Administration présidentielle russe, Maxim Oreshkin, a échangé avec des médias africains lors d’une conférence de presse tenue le 26 octobre 2026. Les échanges ont notamment porté sur les perspectives de coopération entre la Russie et le continent africain, avec un accent particulier sur la souveraineté, le transfert de technologies et le renforcement de l’autonomie économique des États africains. L’Afrique est riche. Elle l’est aussi bien par son potentiel économique que par sa dynamique démographique. C’est la conviction partagée par Maxim Oreshkin. Ce qui est souvent perçu ou présenté comme un défi, le fort taux de natalité, constitue pourtant l'un des leviers stratégiques majeurs du continent, à condition qu'il soit judicieusement exploité. « Le continent africain, c'est l'avenir de l'économie mondiale du point de vue de la démographie et de la dynamique économique. La démographie est un facteur capital pour toute nation », a souligné le responsable politique russe. C’est forts de ce constat et soucieux de valoriser ce potentiel au service du développement continental que plusieurs chefs d’État africains sont attendus à ce 3ᵉ Sommet Russie-Afrique. Dans cette quête constante de leviers de croissance, la Russie entend se tenir aux côtés de l’Afrique pour partager son savoir-faire, sans jamais se substituer aux initiatives locales. Telle est, en substance, la vision portée par Maxim Oreshkin. « La Russie veut que chaque pays africain soit au maximum fort et indépendant. La Russie ne travaille jamais selon le schéma colonial. Elle n'a jamais eu de colonie sur le continent africain. Dans le code occidental, il y a ce schéma : prendre des ressources et générer des revenus. Chez nous, notre code culturel consiste à travailler ensemble autour d'un projet commun », a-t-il soutenu. Formation et transfert technologique : l'exemple du nucléaire égyptien Selon lui, la Russie est prête à accompagner les pays africains dans plusieurs domaines clés comme l’agriculture et l’énergie. Les projets sont conçus et mis en œuvre avec les partenaires selon une approche intégrée. La méthode russe consiste à impliquer les entreprises locales et à former les cadres. L’une des particularités de cette coopération réside dans la valorisation des langues locales lors de la réalisation des projets communs. L’un des exemples emblématiques de ce partenariat est la construction d’une centrale nucléaire en Égypte d'un montant de 25 milliards de dollars. « Je prends l'exemple de l'Égypte. Le grand projet concerne la construction d'un ensemble de blocs d’une centrale nucléaire, couplée à la formation des cadres. Un grand nombre d'étudiants égyptiens, appelés à travailler plus tard sur cette centrale, sont venus en Russie. Ils suivent leur programme, puis ces cursus sont transférés en Égypte où tout un pôle de recherche commence à fonctionner. Tout ce bloc, infrastructures, cadres, sciences, se crée directement sur place, en Égypte. Les partenaires russes accompagnent l'Égypte dans cette démarche », a-t-il expliqué. Le développement de l’Afrique devra également passer par la quête de la souveraineté. Selon le responsable politique russe, cette exigence ne doit pas se limiter au volet politique. Pour lui, la souveraineté numérique est tout aussi cruciale aujourd'hui. Sans elle, la Russie serait devenue « une colonie » d’une autre puissance, estime-t-il. Cela concerne les réseaux sociaux, les messageries, le commerce électronique, la santé publique ou encore l'éducation numérique. Pour l'ensemble de ces outils, la Russie recourt exclusivement à ses propres solutions technologiques. Souveraineté numérique et résilience face aux sanctions « Cela permet à la Russie de ne pas être sous la dépendance d'autres pays, de se sentir en sécurité et de rester indépendante. C'est cette souveraineté que nous souhaitons partager avec nos pays partenaires, en travaillant ensemble pour qu'ils puissent renforcer l'autonomie de leurs propres économies », a-t-il indiqué. Dans la quête de cette souveraineté, les États africains se trouvent toutefois souvent frappés par des sanctions économiques et politiques imposées par des organisations internationales, régionales ou sous-régionales. Le Mali en a fait l'expérience après la prise de pouvoir par le Général d’Armée Assimi Goïta, essuyant les sanctions de la CEDEAO. Comment réussir à faire face à ces restrictions sans renoncer à la quête d'une véritable souveraineté, a interrogé un journaliste soudanais lors de la conférence de presse. « En réalité, les sanctions perturbent très peu de choses. Si vous croyez en vous, si vous croyez en vos partenaires et que vous êtes capables d'avancer, cela devient un stimulant et une source de motivation. Aujourd'hui, la Russie est le pays contre lequel le plus grand nombre de sanctions a été imposé, qu'il s'agisse de personnes morales ou physiques. Mais ce sont plutôt ceux qui les décrètent qui en souffrent le plus », a répondu Maxim Oreshkin. Vers un modèle économique d'endurance partagé Il a rappelé que la Russie avait été sévèrement sanctionnée et que le départ des banques internationales en 2022 avait initialement suscité de l'inquiétude chez les opérateurs économiques et les citoyens. Mais malgré des débuts difficiles, le pays a su s'adapter en réajustant ses partenariats et en créant ses propres leviers économiques, un modèle d'endurance et de résilience que la Russie entend partager avec les États africains. En rappel, cette conférence de presse s’est tenue dans le cadre du Forum économique et humanitaire Russie-Afrique, en marge du Sommet qui sera marqué par la présence du Premier ministre du Burkina Faso, Rimtalba Jean-Emmanuel Ouédraogo, représentant du président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré. Amadou ZEBA Envoyé spécial à Moscou L’article Russie-Afrique : Moscou défend un modèle de coopération fondé sur l’indépendance des États est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Flu cases double at Karachi hospitals in over a week amid seasonal shift
items.description: • JPMC, CHK report more cases over past 10 days than first half of month • Experts advise frequent hand washing, avoiding close contact with sick people and staying hydrated KARACHI: The city is seeing a spike in the number of flu cases over the past eight to 10 days, senior health experts shared on Monday, urging people to take precautionary measures to cope with changing weather conditions. “We have been seeing patients with flu-like symptoms for over a month but their numbers have just doubled over the past week, rising from 30 to 40 per day to 70 to 80 now, with the gradual seasonal shift towards winter, especially the drop in night-time temperatures,” said Dr Irfan Siddiqui, heading the emergency department of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC). He said, “At the initial stages [of illness], people generally turn to clinics in their neighbourhoods, and it’s only when the disease takes a serious turn that they report to a hospital’s emergency department”. He added that the large number of cases at one of the city’s key tertiary care hospitals indicated that a far greater number of people are being affected in the city and the number of patients visiting the hospital was just the tip of the iceberg. JPMC, CHK report more cases over past 10 days than first half of month The spike in flu cases, he said, was seasonal and that people with weak immune systems, the elderly and children, were more vulnerable. Another factor contributing to the spike, he pointed out, was the general public’s reluctance to adapt their eating habits to changing weather conditions, which could make them more susceptible to illness. Most flu patients currently reporting to the hospital, he said, were aged between 18 and 32 years and belonged to the labour class. A significant number of them were heavy smokers and drug users. “Patients are generally presenting with severe illness and taking a longer-than-usual time for recovery,” he added. Dr Siddiqui emphasised the need to practise good hygiene and maintain healthy habits. He advised people to wash their hands frequently, stay at home when ill, avoid close contact with sick people, stay hydrated and get adequate sleep. He also advised against consuming cold drinks and water. “Getting a flu shot every year [early fall] is the most effective step to reduce the risk of seasonal flu and potential complications. But the vaccine is costly and available only at private healthcare settings.” As at JPMC, the number of flu patients reporting to Dr Ruth Pfau Civil Hospital Karachi (CHK) has doubled in just over a week. “The cases have jumped from eight-10 [a day] to 30 to 40. This includes people of all age groups, though younger people aged 20-30 are dominant,” said Dr Imran Sarwar, additional medical superintendent and head of the emergency department at CHK. “Perhaps it’s more contagious this time as we are getting three to five patients of the same family,” he said, adding that flu treatment was symptomatic, with only a few complicated cases requiring admission. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

Ebola fight: Misinformation is our worst enemy — GHS boss
items.description: The Director-General of the Ghana Health Service (GHS), Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, has warned that misinformation could undermine Ghana’s efforts to prepare for a possible Ebola outbreak, urging journalists and social media users to verify information before publishing or sharing it. He has appealed to the media, content creators and users of platforms such as TikTok and WhatsApp to rely on official sources for updates on the disease, cautioning that inaccurate or misleading reports could complicate public health communication at a time when clear, credible information is critical. “Our worst enemy is misinformation,” Dr Akoriyea said on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, October 26. He urged the public to cross-check claims with the Ghana Health Service and the Ministry of Health before circulating them. “Ghana Health Service website is there, the Ministry of Health website is there, the Minister is there, I’m there, we have PROs, cross-check before you come out,” he appealed. The GHS Director-General said the speed at which information circulates online made verification especially important, as people could easily misrepresent health developments or spread claims that had not been confirmed. “In this era, people miscommunicate a lot,” he added. Dr Akoriyea said Ghana had intensified its preparedness measures to strengthen its ability to respond if an Ebola case were detected, although the true test of readiness would come when the country had to manage an actual case. “We have increased our preparedness to make sure that we tighten all the knots,” he said. “Until we get a case, we might not be able to prove our readiness and even no matter how ready you are, no matter how ready you are, when you get a case, it’s a different story.” He said it was nevertheless better for the country to prepare thoroughly before a possible outbreak than to be caught unprepared. “But it’s better to be prepared, right, and get a case and do commit very few errors than not to be prepared at all,” he said. The Director-General cited Ghana’s experience during the COVID-19 pandemic as an important foundation for strengthening its response to future health emergencies. He said the availability of the Ga East Municipal Hospital and the University of Ghana Medical Centre (UGMC) had been an advantage during the pandemic, adding that lessons from that period were informing efforts to improve the country’s preparedness. “I remember we were extremely prepared, and we’re so fortunate as a country during COVID that we had Ga East already built, we had UGMC already built, and we are building on that to make sure that whatever we have done or we had done, now we can even make it better,” he said. Trusted information critical The appeal comes amid heightened concern over Ebola and the need for countries to strengthen surveillance, preparedness and public communication as outbreaks are reported in parts of Africa. Ebola is a severe viral disease that can spread through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person who is showing symptoms, or with contaminated materials. Prompt identification, isolation and appropriate care of suspected cases, alongside effective contact tracing and infection prevention, are important to containing transmission. Public health authorities also rely on accurate information to explain risks, clarify what is known about an outbreak and communicate recommended precautions. False claims can fuel fear, undermine trust in health authorities and encourage people to act on advice that has not been medically verified.

items.title: Minister blames closure of border for LPG price hike
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The National Assembly was apprised on Monday that closure of Pakistan-Iran border was one of the main reasons of sky rocketing price of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) in the country. “Closure of Pak-Iran border is one of the main reasons of high prices of LPG and now we are trying to get the fuel from sea route,” said Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervez Malik while responding to a calling attention notice in the house. The notice, which was jointly moved by Ms Aliya Kamran, Shahida Begum and Naeema Kishwar Khan, invited the attention of minister to a matter of urgent public importance regarding unprecedented increase in the prices of LPG causing grave concern among the public. A mover of the bill Aliya Kamran said in remote and northern areas of the country the LPG was selling at Rs 700 to Rs 800 per kg against its official price, set by Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) of Rs 280 per kg. LPG is largely consumed fuel in remote and far flung areas of the country where pipe gas is not available. The consumption of LPG and its price increase in winter. Naeema Kishwar questioned that why the government has suspended trade with Iran through border. On this the minister said 50 to 60pc LPG was imported from Iran and rest of the required fuel we get from Qatar. He said due to United States-Iran war LPG supply from Qatar has been suspended. He said the government was reviewing the whole system and that it has a policy to acquir the gas from other sources abroad. The minister also agreed the official price of LPG, prescribed by Ogra was Rs 280 per kg. However, it has been observed that even during surplus supply of LPG, the gas is nowhere sold at the government rate. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026
