items.title: Un sombrero ‘cowboy’ para Aznar, un ladrillo de una cárcel para Zapatero y un boli bala para Rajoy: los sorprendentes regalos a los presidentes
items.description: Los camellos que rodean a la jaima de Muamar El Gadafi en Trípoli (Libia) son solo un espejismo. “Dios mío”, exclama José María Aznar, entonces presidente del Gobierno (1996-2004), cuando ve a Najar el Jayed, El Rayo del Líder, un purasangre enjaezado que le acaba de regalar Gadafi ( 2003 ). El caballo acaba en España, como ocurre años después con la silla de montar con la que Gadafi agasaja a José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (2004-2011) . El listado de los obsequios recibidos por el expresidente socialista está ahora en el centro de la polémica: el magistrado José Luis Calama ha solicitado a Patrimonio Nacional que le remita el inventario completo tras encontrar joyas en la caja fuerte del despacho del exlíder del PSOE durante la investigación del caso Plus Ultra. Zapatero las atribuye a un obsequio personal del monarca saudí Abdalá Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud . Pero el registro oficial de los regalos recibidos por los expresidentes del siglo XXI, al que accedió este diario en aplicación de la ley de transparencia, no las recoge. En contraste, sí muestra una mezcla de objetos de lujo y diseñados para sorprender o para retratar una época. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El cierre de la librería Pérgamo no es lo que parece: ni especulación, ni fondos buitres, ni otro ‘caso Maricarmen’
items.description: La librería más antigua de Madrid protagoniza estos días un thriller inmobiliario en el que no todo es lo que parece. Para contar la historia que hay detrás, hay que presentar a sus tres protagonistas: la dueña del local y de la librería, Ana Serrano, una mujer que heredó el negocio de su familia y que lo regentó junto a su hermana toda la vida; Juan José Janeiro, un inversor extranjero que aprovechó el momento en que se anunció el cierre hace algo más de cuatro años y quiso rescatarla; y Pablo Cerezo, un joven entusiasta comprometido con la cultura. El conflicto amenaza con hacer desaparecer Pérgamo, una librería con estanterías de otro siglo y por la que han pasado los autores más reconocidos del mundo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fue un experimento en los años 50 y ahora es el peor barrio de Madrid: 408 pisos de 40 metros cuadrados casi en ruina
items.description: En Villaverde Alto hay 800 personas que viven en chabolas verticales. Es la Colonia Experimental, una isla abandonada construida en los años cincuenta para alojar provisionalmente a familias procedentes de otras provincias, principalmente de Andalucía y Extremadura. Son 408 pisos del tamaño de una caja de zapatos. Miden de media 34 metros cuadrados, las humedades pintan de negro las zonas comunes, en las paredes las grietas parten a la mitad los edificios, los techos son de dos metros de alto, las calles son barrizales sin asfaltar y las fachadas de los edificios se caen literalmente a pedazos. El Ayuntamiento de Madrid las ha catalogado como infraviviendas porque no reúnen las condiciones mínimas de habitabilidad y los vecinos, aunque ya esperan la primera fase para el derribo y reconstrucción, siguen viviendo un infierno todos los días. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Raquel Zas: “Cuando pensamos en una mujer que rechaza el sexo siempre pensamos en un gran trauma”
items.description: Los años secos (Temas de hoy) sigue la trayectoria de Clara, una joven que vuelve a su pueblo después de romper con su novio. Un viaje que le sirve para desentrañar los posibles motivos de su rechazo al sexo . La comunicadora y periodista Raquel Zas (Viveiro, 1989) encontró la inspiración para esta, su primera novela, en el documental Venus: confesiones desnudas, en el que cien mujeres hablan de sus experiencias sexuales. El desequilibrio entre cantidad y calidad de los encuentros que relataban las entrevistadas encendió la chispa de su creatividad y retomó un manuscrito empezado y abandonado en 2020. La autora ha reflexionado mucho sobre “cuánto de lo que consideramos deseo es propio” y a través de Clara indaga en esa cuestión pero también en las diferencias de clase social, el valor de la amistad o las relaciones familiares. Siempre con un poco de retranca, como buena gallega. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El siluro, “un pez monstruo” invasor de dos metros, vacía el mayor pantano de Andalucía de carpas y barbos
items.description: La primera vez que se documentó de forma oficial que el siluro ―especie exótica invasora― nadaba por el pantano de Iznájar (Córdoba), el mayor de Andalucía, fue en 2011 . Pero los pescadores ya habían detectado años antes, en 2003, la presencia de ejemplares pequeños de medio kilo. No se trata de un pez cualquiera: puede superar los dos metros y pesar 100 kilos, como algunos de los ejemplares que se pescan ahora allí. Y tiene un apetito voraz, ya que se estima que consumen diariamente entre un 2% y un 4% de su peso; en los ejemplares de mayor tamaño, equivale a entre dos y cuatro kilos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Quemar la ciudad
items.description: Durante más de dos décadas hemos sostenido una ficción que consistía en negarnos a nosotros mismos que las leyes y regulaciones que limitaban la vida real pudieran aplicarse en la vida digital. Algunos llamaron a eso un nuevo Salvaje Oeste, con sus pistoleros, sus pillajes, sus linchamientos y sus saloons . Tarde, y a regañadientes, algunos padres comprendieron que sus hijas no podían ser desnudadas por inteligencia artificial en las redes para burla de sus compañeros de instituto y quizá algún día los partidos políticos entenderán que cuando fabrican sus vídeos falsos para desacreditar a los rivales electorales tan sólo contribuyen a la degradación de una sociedad que ha visto cómo la utopía digital se transformaba en una pesadilla. Ese quemar la calle virtual se ha trasladado a una oleada de disturbios y destrucción callejera. Amparada bajo las protestas generales en muchas capitales europeas por la carestía de la vivienda y los bajos salarios, por redes sociales se convocó a los jóvenes a ponerse ropa negra y arramplar con el mobiliario urbano y asaltar las tiendas de producto informático, ropa y zapatillas de marca. Los intereses tan específicos de ese pillaje delatan que los altercados consisten en reivindicar el derecho a una posesión de unos bienes tan deseados como sobrevalorados. El experimento social llevado a cabo en estos años ha fracasado, por eso cuanto antes lo reconozcamos más tiempo tendremos para comenzar a enderezarlo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los vaqueros de ‘La Pedra’
items.description: Cuando escucho al Apretao de Amurrio decir con el pecho p’afuera que él se llevaría los desfiles del Orgullo a un polígono industrial y al Lupitas asturiano, con esas ínfulas de dandy negrero, atreverse a cuestionar las sacrosantas pensiones, no sé ni lo que siento: una cosa que pasa mucho con este neofascismo de horteras hiperbólicos que nos ha tocado vivir es que se quedan cortas no ya las palabras sino también las emociones; tanto que deberían hacer una tercera parte de Inside Out , esa película que explicaba a los niños la alegría, la tristeza, la ira, el miedo y el asco. Necesitamos pistas sobre qué es esta mezcla de estupor y despersonalización que sobreviene cuando se escuchan esas burradas que insultan primero a muchos de nuestros amigos y luego a nuestros padres. Pero no hay tregua. Aparece el destructor de Os Peares , cada día más sinsonio , opinando sobre el aborto de las niñas de 16 años y queda claro que la cosa es grave, muy grave, no solo porque de nuevo hay retrógrados queriendo adueñarse de nuestros coños sino porque me siento incapaz de darle importancia a qué llevan puesto: echo de menos cuando los vestidos de Melania eran herramienta de comunicación y Pablo Iglesias, quien presumía de sus camisas de Alcampo, se hacía un esmoquin a medida en las páginas de Vanity Fair . Ahora me doy cuenta de que aquel margen para el soft power era síntoma de salud democrática. Pero estamos a las puertas de los años treinta, y conforme a una tradición capitalista instaurada hace cien años, en esta década el sistema peta porque los billonarios se lo quedan todo, el consumo se gripa y muere el optimismo. Los vaqueros que Pedro Sánchez llevaba otro día eran espantosos y baratos , eso sí lo percibí, lo que me dio paz porque le conferían pinta de hombre normal. Iba con ellos puestos cuando una mujer maravillosa con modos de cupletista le llamó “Pedra”. Fue muy gracioso pero yo no pude reírme porque últimamente no sé ni qué siento.

items.description: Shaibu Dauda Abdulai, the Ellembelle National Democratic Congress (NDC) Constituency Chairman-elect, has pledged to unite and reconcile party faithful to retain power in December 2028. He made his intentions and vision clear in a statement after his victory in last Saturday’s Ellembelle NDC Constituency election at Ampain in the Western Region. “Comrades, the campaign is over. The election is over. Now is the time to heal wounds, reconcile and bring everybody on board,” the statement said. Mr Abdulai, popularly called Vanda, expressed special appreciation to Mr Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, the Member of Parliament for Ellembelle; Mr Joseph Armah Agyekum, the District Chief Executive for the area; delegates and all members at the 160 branches for the peace, transparency and fairness which characterised the polls. He noted that this was ample testimony that internal democracy had been entrenched in the NDC as a party and, by extension, as the government. Mr Abdulai, who is the Personal Assistant to the Member of Parliament, Mr Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, acknowledged the efforts of delegates who “stood in long queues, sacrificed your time, resources and voted for hope, unity and progress”. He said, “I do not take this mandate for granted. I promise to lead with respect and dignity for every branch.” Outlining his vision for the party, the Ellembelle NDC Chairman-elect pledged to serve as Chairman for all and to run an open-door, all-inclusive administration. Mr Abdulai promised, “to work in total loyalty and support for the MP, DCE and all stakeholders to make the Ellembelle NDC more attractive, united and strong and work hard to retain the Ellembelle seat and increase votes come 2028.”

items.title: Privatisation framework
items.description: THE proposed merger of the Privatisation Commission and the Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A) into a single institution is a sensible move. It will end the duality of functions and provide a more coherent framework for mobilising private capital to manage public assets and develop physical infrastructure for which the state has limited resources to spare. Although the two bodies operate under separate laws, their mandates intersect in bringing private capital and expertise into areas dominated by the state. A unified entity could offer a common platform for evaluating these options. Privatisation involves transferring ownership or control of state assets, while public-private partnerships (PPPs) allow governments to enlist private capital for projects they cannot finance. Both approaches require sound financial assessments and clear risk allocations. With Pakistan facing persistent fiscal constraints, the state cannot afford to finance loss-making enterprises indefinitely. Private investment can help ease these pressures, but it is not an end in itself. Poorly structured transactions can leave the state with inadequate returns or costly contractual obligations. The proposed legislation envisages four public funds to support privatisation and PPP transactions. These instruments could help prepare viable projects and attract investment. However, they must not become vehicles for subsidising commercially unsound ventures. Government guarantees and liabilities should be disclosed and assessed before deals are approved. The proposed legal protections for serving and former officials acting in good faith also require careful rethinking. Officials should be protected against frivolous litigation when making decisions in the public interest. Such protection must not, however, become immunity from accountability. Making PPP agreements accessible as public documents is also positive. Public scrutiny is particularly important when private investors enter long-term arrangements that may impose financial obligations on taxpayers and successive governments. The new arrangement offers an opportunity to improve the management of state assets and infrastructure investment. Its success will depend on securing fair value for public property, attracting credible investors and ensuring that partnerships deliver tangible benefits. The bill proposes a majority-independent board with private-sector representation to strengthen commercial decision-making. Its effectiveness will require transparent appointments, relevant expertise, political independence, clear performance benchmarks, strong accountability, and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules to ensure effective governance. The state must now ensure that commercial discipline, transparency and accountability guide its implementation. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

items.title: La nueva edad dorada del cocido madrileño: el plato tradicional convive con versiones cada vez más sofisticadas
items.description: “Es una revolución”, asegura Rogelio Enríquez, presidente de la Academia Madrileña de Gastronomía, cuando se le pregunta por esa línea de cocidos que pone en valor el origen de los ingredientes y va mucho más allá de los dos y tres vuelcos tradicionales. Ahora mismo, en Madrid, la receta vive una nueva edad dorada, con aproximaciones que están elevando el plato de toda la vida —que, evidentemente, continúa en su formato más tradicional y accesible en los menús del día, las casas de comidas y los restaurantes especializados—. “El cocido es el primer menú degustación de la historia”, defiende Enríquez. La demanda, además, atraviesa un buen momento. “La gente cada vez cocina menos en casa. Entonces, ir a comer un cocido es ya un hito en sí mismo”. Como cocidos inquietos, hoy ya desaparecidos, Enríquez indica el de Iván Sáez en Desencaja, hoy en el Club de Campo, “muy historiado, con las carnes muy trabajadas”; o el que hacían Manuel Domínguez y Mary Morales en Lúa , “un cocido gallego con un punto de sofisticación y ceremonia”. items.title: Ghana explores AI to predict Ebola and other health threats — GHS
items.description: The Ghana Health Service (GHS) is exploring the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to help anticipate disease outbreaks and strengthen emergency planning as the country steps up preparations against the threat of Ebola. The Director-General of the GHS, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, said health officials were considering how emerging technologies could improve the assessment of public health risks and support timely decisions when infectious diseases threaten to cross national borders. He said the discussions formed part of broader preparedness efforts following reports of Ebola outbreaks in parts of Africa and concerns about the potential spread of the disease through international travel. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, October 26, Dr Kaba Akoriyea said the proposed use of AI was intended to help authorities better anticipate developments and plan their response. “From there, I move into a meeting where we are talking about technology and how to even use AI to help predict what will happen,” he revealed. Technology to support early warning The exploration of AI comes as public health authorities face the challenge of identifying infectious disease threats in a world where people travel frequently between countries and outbreaks can have implications beyond the communities in which they begin. Predictive technologies can help analyse information such as disease trends, population movement and environmental conditions to identify emerging risks and guide decisions on where surveillance and resources may be needed. For Ghana, such tools could potentially complement existing disease monitoring systems by helping officials identify areas requiring closer attention and plan interventions before a health emergency escalates. However, the effectiveness of AI-based systems would depend on the availability of reliable and timely data, appropriate technical expertise and the capacity of health authorities to act on the information generated. The technology would not replace laboratory diagnosis, clinical assessment or established outbreak response measures. Rather, it could serve as an additional tool to support decisions by public health officials. Ghana remains in preparedness phase Dr Kaba Akoriyea stressed that Ghana was preparing for a possible Ebola threat, rather than announcing the detection of an outbreak in the country. “But now, let me say that when it comes to Ebola, we are in the face of preparedness,” he noted. The GHS has reported conducting simulation exercises and coordinating with other state institutions as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s response arrangements. The Director-General has also described the work of the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre at Pantang, which monitors international health developments and supports emergency coordination. The preparedness effort involves multiple agencies, including those responsible for health, security, education and disaster management, reflecting the need for a coordinated response if a suspected case is identified. Ghana’s regional engagements are also important because of the movement of people across borders and the need for countries to share information about emerging health risks. Surveillance remains critical Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause serious illness and death. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person who is symptomatic or with contaminated materials. Symptoms may develop between two and 21 days after exposure. Consequently, a person who has been infected may not appear ill when travelling, making surveillance, accurate traveller information and appropriate follow-up important elements of outbreak preparedness. Public health responses typically involve the rapid identification and assessment of suspected cases, laboratory testing, isolation and clinical care where indicated, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, and public education.

items.title: Meta prévoit de lever 35 milliards de dollars pour financer sa course à l’IA
items.description: La maison mère de Facebook, Instagram et WhatsApp prévoit une augmentation de capital de 35 milliards de dollars, sa première depuis son introduction en Bourse en 2012. Le groupe de Mark Zuckerberg envisage également un programme supplémentaire d’émission d’actions pouvant atteindre 60 milliards de dollars, alors que ses investissements pourraient grimper jusqu’à 145 milliards en 2026. Meta accélère la mobilisation de ressources financières pour soutenir ses ambitions dans l’intelligence artificielle (IA). Le groupe américain prévoit de lever 35 milliards de dollars à travers une augmentation de capital, selon des documents publiés lundi auprès de la Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), l’autorité américaine des marchés financiers. La maison mère de Facebook, Instagram et WhatsApp envisage également de lancer un programme supplémentaire d’émission d’actions, pour un montant maximal de 60 milliards de dollars. La date de mise en œuvre de cette opération n’a pas encore été précisée. Cette augmentation de capital constitue une première pour le groupe californien depuis son introduction en Bourse, en mai 2012. Parmi les acteurs susceptibles de participer à l’opération figurent les fabricants de puces Nvidia, AMD et Broadcom. Selon l’un des documents déposés auprès de la SEC, ces entreprises ont manifesté leur intérêt pour l’acquisition d’une partie des nouvelles actions, à hauteur de 5 milliards de dollars au total. Cette initiative intervient alors que Meta a récemment annoncé vouloir mobiliser des « centaines de milliards de dollars » sur plusieurs années pour développer ses capacités en intelligence artificielle. Lors de la présentation de ses résultats mercredi dernier, le groupe avait indiqué vouloir commencer à lever ces fonds dès l’automne. Des investissements pouvant atteindre 145 milliards de dollars en 2026 Les besoins financiers de Meta reflètent l’ampleur des investissements nécessaires pour développer les infrastructures de l’IA. Le groupe prévoit de consacrer entre 135 et 145 milliards de dollars à ses dépenses d’investissement en 2026, principalement pour la construction et le développement de centres de données, essentiels à l’entraînement et au fonctionnement des modèles d’intelligence artificielle. Jusqu’à présent, les grandes entreprises technologiques, dont Meta, Alphabet, Microsoft et Amazon, ont largement financé leurs investissements dans l’IA grâce à leur trésorerie. Mais l’augmentation des dépenses liées à cette course technologique pousse désormais certains acteurs à rechercher des financements extérieurs. Meta a déjà levé plusieurs dizaines de milliards de dollars sur les marchés obligataires. Le groupe entend désormais compléter ses ressources par des émissions d’actions, alors que la compétition pour développer des infrastructures et des technologies d’IA toujours plus puissantes s’intensifie. Cette stratégie traduit le poids croissant des investissements dans l’intelligence artificielle pour les géants technologiques, confrontés à des besoins de financement considérables afin de soutenir leurs ambitions à long terme. The post Meta prévoit de lever 35 milliards de dollars pour financer sa course à l’IA appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Refining Ghanaian crude in Ghana keeps value onshore – TOR MD
items.description: Edmond Kombat, Managing Director (MD) of the Tema Oil Refinery (TOR), underscored the strategic importance of refining Ghanaian crude oil domestically, calling it a critical step toward retaining value in the national economy and fulfilling the President’s value-addition vision. “Refining Ghanaian crude in Ghana keeps value onshore. It fulfils the value addition vision of the President for Ghana,” Mr Kombat said in his remarks at the Government Accountability Press Conference, at the Jubilee House in Accra. He said the turnaround maintenance ran from August 1 to October 30, 2025, adding that after the maintenance works were completed, the National Petroleum Authority (NPA) inspected the plant, confirmed compliance with mandatory safety and operational requirements, and cleared TOR to resume refining. He said crude processing started on December 19, 2025, with all product streams going to storage for the first time in years. Mr Kombat said since May 2026, TOR has received four five-million-barrel crude cargoes: Bonga, Baleine, Bonnie Light, and, on July 15, Ghana’s Jubilee Medium Sweet crude, an indigenous crude delivered aboard MT Apache. He said the TOR paid in full for the Jubilee cargo, making it the refinery’s first Jubilee cargo in a decade. The MD said the President commissioned the refurbished Crude Distillation Unit on August 1, 2026. Mr Kombat said the refinery then received another parcel of Ghanaian indigenous crude, 950,000 barrels of Sankofa crude, on 25 September 2026 from our sister agency, the Ghana National Petroleum Company (GNPC). He noted that the refinery’s operations now represent a landmark achievement in the country’s petroleum sector. “We are witnessing Ghanaian crude being refined by Ghanaian engineers in a Ghanaian refinery, effectively linking the Ghanaian petroleum upstream, midstream and downstream together,” he said. The MD highlighted the role of strategic offtake partnerships in strengthening the domestic refining ecosystem. “Our offtake partnerships, including our engagement with GOIL on the 2026 arrangement, were intended to increase the supply of locally refined products, improve security of supply, and support greater price stability at the pump,” he explained. He further disclosed that, but for the restoration of TOR and other government-supported domestic production, fuel prices in the last two pricing windows could have sold between GHS22 and GHS32 per litre. Mr Kombat said the revamp of TOR guaranteed Ghana and its Sahelian Neighbours Fuel Security and Availability. He said TOR’s close working relationship with the National Petroleum Authority, Bulk Oil Storage and Transportation Company Limited (BOST), and other Petroleum Service providers has increased Burkina Faso’s National Oil Company’s petroleum product movement through Ghana from 15 per cent in 2024 to 40 per cent as at today. On expansion and work ahead, Mr Kombat said engineers from Verga Engineering are working with TOR’s technical team to complete the tie-in and commission the F-61 this month. This, he said, would allow the Crude Distillation Unit to move from its current throughput of about 28,000 bpd to its nameplate capacity of 45,000 bpd to 55,000 bpd. In the medium term, they plan to install a new air cooler to raise capacity to 60,000 bpd and replace the 6,500 barrel-a-day catalytic reformers with a 10,000 barrel-per-day continuous catalytic reformer. He noted that the new 120-ton boiler had been installed, while work on the RFCC turnaround and SCADA system continues. Mr Kombat said on August 1, the President directed the Minister of Energy and Green Transition to work with the TOR Board and Management on a strategic roadmap to raise processing capacity to 100,000 barrels a day, with a further plan to increase it to 200,000 barrels per day as the end state. He also announced plans to restructure TOR so that it could operate on sound commercial principles, without political interference.

items.title: Your past prescriptions haven’t helped developing countries – TOR MD tells IMF
items.description: Edmond Kombat, the Managing Director of the Tema Oil Refinery Limited (TOR), has challenged the International Monetary Fund (IMF) over its long-standing prescriptions for state-owned enterprises. He noted that the Fund appears to be revising its literature because its past advice “hasn’t helped” developing countries. Mr Kombat responded to a question about the reason for the recent visit by an IMF delegation to the state-owned Oil Refinery at the Government Accountability Series Press Conference held at the Presidency in Accra. Mr Kombat said the Fund had written extensively about Ghana’s energy sector, including TOR. He traced the country’s history with IMF-backed programmes—from the Economic Recovery Programme to the Financial Sector Recovery Programme and the Divestiture of State Enterprises—and observed that the Fund had traditionally promoted private business and “usually they don’t like state entities running businesses.” “But it looks like they are changing their literature, because most of those prescriptions that they give actually haven’t helped the developing countries,” he said. He said in Ghana, state-owned enterprises were beginning to show that state institutions could work and work very well. “And we were happy to receive them and show them that under His Excellency President John Dramani Mahama, state entities are working, and are working profitably, and are not the loss-making entities,” Mr Kombat added. He noted that the IMF delegation seemed impressed, reiterating that “but we also remain guarded.”

items.title: Ghana activates Ebola preparedness system, conducts simulation exercises — GHS
items.description: The Ghana Health Service (GHS) says it has activated its preparedness arrangements for Ebola and conducted simulation exercises as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s ability to respond to a possible outbreak. The Director-General of the GHS, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, said the institution was monitoring developments across affected countries and coordinating with relevant institutions to assess potential risks to Ghana. He said the country had intensified surveillance and emergency planning following reports of Ebola outbreaks in parts of Africa, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, as well as concerns about possible cross-border transmission. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, October 26, Dr Kaba Akoriyea said Ghana was in the preparedness phase and had begun testing its response arrangements through simulation exercises. “So here you are, you have an outbreak in Congo, Uganda, and then you see it coming to Kenya, and we have airlines that come indirectly, day in, day out. Then from there, you see it get to Nigeria. And as I talk to you, I’m always in touch with my colleagues in those countries to know exactly what is happening,” he explained. Emergency operations centre on alert Dr Kaba Akoriyea said the GHS was using its Public Health Emergency Operations Centre at Pantang to monitor international health developments and coordinate preparedness activities. He said the centre operated around the clock, allowing health officials to track emerging threats and respond to developments that could have implications for Ghana. “We’ve put it out there all the time. Every second, microsecond of the day, we scan, and we know exactly what is happening in any part of the world. It’s there,” he sated. “You can go and see. We don’t sleep, work 24 hours, and we see whatever is happening.” The Director-General said the Service had carried out about three simulation exercises since concerns about the disease emerged in the region, adding that preparedness activities had begun earlier when the outbreak in the DRC was reported. “Yesterday, I’ll tell you, we’ve already done about three simulation exercises since we heard of the issue in Kenya. “When it started in DRC, we activated our system. In Congo, in Kenya, we started with simulation exercise.” Simulation exercises are used to test how institutions would coordinate their response to a public health emergency, including the identification and management of suspected cases, communication between agencies and the mobilisation of resources. 33 agencies involved in preparedness Dr Kaba Akoriyea said Ghana’s preparations involved a broad range of institutions beyond the health sector, reflecting the need for a coordinated response if an outbreak occurred. He said he had attended meetings involving agencies responsible for education, security, social welfare, local government and emergency management. “And today, alone, I have gone to meetings where we have cross-border issues. “And I can provide you with the list, and you can cross-check. You have education, you have military, you have police, you have welfare, you have local government, you have all the necessary agencies, present including NADMO, you have them all, about 33 agencies.” He named the Food and Drugs Authority, the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO), the National Commission for Civic Education, the Ghana Education Service, the Veterinary Services Department, the National Peace Council and the Ghana Armed Forces among the institutions involved. The involvement of multiple agencies is intended to support coordination in areas such as emergency response, public communication, security, logistics and the management of people who may be affected by a health emergency. Cross-border cooperation The GHS Director-General said Ghana was also working with neighbouring countries to strengthen cooperation on infectious diseases and other health threats that could move across borders. He cited recent engagements with counterparts in Burkina Faso and Côte d’Ivoire, as well as a tripartite meeting to compare developments and discuss possible responses. He said the meetings were particularly important because of the movement of people across borders and the need for countries to share information promptly. “So we’ve held a cross-border meeting with our counterparts in Burkina, we’ve had one with our counterparts in Côte d’Ivoire, Ivory Coast, and we’ve had a tripartite meeting to know what is happening there and what is happening here. How do we compare those and solve these issues?”

items.title: Ebola: Ghana has not dropped the ball on disease screening – Prof Amuasi
items.description: Prof John Amuasi, Leader of Global Health at the KCCR, has rejected suggestions that Ghana has let its disease screening systems slip since the COVID-19 pandemic. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, he said screening at entry points must match the prevailing risk. He argued that testing every arriving traveller for Ebola would be impractical. “No, I wouldn’t say so,” he said when asked whether Ghana had dropped the ball. His comments come after Nigeria confirmed an imported Ebola case on October 20. The patient developed symptoms four days after arriving from Uganda. Investigations into the source of infection remain ongoing, according to the World Health Organisation. Elsewhere, Kenya had recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths as of October 25. Uganda also recorded cases earlier in the outbreak, but the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says its outbreak has ended. Prof Amuasi said the Nigerian case illustrated the limits of airport screening. “There is no way that the Nigerian authorities could have caught this at the airport unless they were doing an active test of everybody coming in to see if they had Ebola, which is simply not practicable.” He explained that highly intensive screening cannot be maintained every day without a clear reason. He said the immediate priority should be stronger information gathering and better guidance for travellers. “So this is why I’m saying that for now, what needs to be done, and I hope it is being done, is to augment the data collection on every single individual who comes.” He acknowledged that collecting more information could raise privacy concerns. But he stressed its importance. “It may be a bit intrusive, but is very critical,” he said. Prof Amuasi also proposed giving arriving travellers leaflets. These should explain symptoms to watch for, whom to contact and where to seek care if they become ill. His defence of the screening approach came with a qualification. He called for stronger data collection but did not confirm whether it was already happening. He said a confirmed case would require a different response. “But beyond that, any other measure is not very helpful at this point. If we did have a case, it would change the dynamics entirely.”

items.title: Egypt: Drop Charges Against Prominent Journalist
items.description: Click to expand Image Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, in Cairo, Egypt, November 24, 2017. © 2017 Roger Anis/AP Photo (Beirut) – Egyptian authorities should drop their case against Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Mada Masr, ahead of her October 27, 2026 hearing, Human Rights Watch said today. The Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP) referred Attalah for trial on October 22 in Case No. 9072/2026 on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license. The referral came the day after prosecutors questioned her over the outlet’s reporting. She faces a fine of up to 3 million Egyptian pounds (about US$53,400) as well as the closure of Mada Masr and confiscation of its equipment. “The hasty prosecution of Lina Attalah marks another escalation in Egyptian authorities’ outrageous attack on independent media in the country,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “No journalist should face criminal prosecution for doing their job.” On October 19, prosecutors summoned Attalah for questioning. On October 21, they questioned Attalah over allegations of publishing “false news” and operating a website without a license, then released her on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds (about $1,780). The following day, prosecutors referred her for trial on charges of operating the website without a license. According to Mada Masr, this is the sixth case brought against the outlet or its journalists in the past six years. Egypt’s 2018 Press and Media Regulation Law requires websites operating in Egypt to obtain a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. The law allows the council to suspend or block websites operating without a valid license. Mada Masr reported that it applied for a license in 2018 and again in 2020. It said that the authorities rejected its application without notifying it and that the platform had challenged that rejection in court. In 2023, Mada Masr submitted a new application with additional documents, and the authorities have not yet responded. Attalah’s prosecution raises concerns about the use of licensing requirements to restrict independent media, Human Rights Watch said. Arbitrary licensing rejections or weaponizing licensing requirements by failing to respond promptly to good faith efforts to comply and forcing entities into legal limbo violates international human rights law. Egyptian authorities have repeatedly targeted Attalah and Mada Masr. In September 2022, prosecutors questioned Attalah and three Mada Masr journalists over allegations of publishing false news, disturbing public peace, and harming public interest. In November 2023, prosecutors summoned Attalah for questioning following an investigation by the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. In August 2025, prosecutors again questioned Attalah over allegations of publishing “false news” and operating a website without a license, following Mada Masr’s reporting on alleged abuses at Badr 3 prison. More than a hundred civil society organizations, including Human Rights Watch, have called on Egyptian authorities to end the prosecution of Attalah and grant Mada Masr a license to operate. Attalah’s prosecution comes amid a broader crackdown on independent media in Egypt and less than a month after security forces arrested six journalists working for the independent investigative journalism platform Matsda2sh on September 28 and 29, 2026. The journalists, who constituted the platform’s entire editorial newsroom, remain in pretrial detention facing charges of “joining and financing a terrorist group,” “spreading false news,” and using social media to disseminate it. Some of them have since alleged that the authorities tortured them in detention and attempted to extract coerced confessions, according to their lawyers. The authorities should drop all charges stemming from exercising the right to freedom of expression and end their repeated harassment of independent media, Human Rights Watch said. Egypt remains one of the world’s leading jailers of journalists, with 25 journalists behind bars as of early October, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Egyptian authorities have blocked access to Mada Masr’s website in Egypt since May 2017. Egypt is obligated under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights to respect freedom of expression, including press freedom. The United Nations Human Rights Committee, which authoritatively interprets the covenant, has found that governments may not prohibit a site or an information dissemination system from publishing material solely on the basis that it may be critical of the government. “Setting registration requirements and then repeatedly ignoring Mada Masr’s good faith attempts to fulfill them is a transparent attempt by authorities to undermine the platform and violates international human rights law,” Khawaja said. “The Egyptian authorities should drop the charges and end the ongoing crackdown on independent journalism.”

items.title: CDABI president launches two books on digital asset regulation
items.description: President of the Chamber of Digital Assets and Blockchain Innovations (CDABI), Ghana Chapter, Dr Caleb Kwaku Afaglo, has launched two books on digital asset regulation to inform policy decisions and industry development in Ghana and West Africa. The books were soft-launched in Accra on Thursday, October 22, 2026, on the opening day of MOBEX Africa 2026. They are “Global Digital Asset Regulation Read from Accra: A Reference Report for Ghana and West Africa” and “Rules for a New Money: Building Digital Asset Regulation from Accra”. The main launch is scheduled for Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 0930 hours at the Africa Stablecoin Summit in Cape Town, South Africa. CDABI, in partnership with Vessel & Light Publishing, published the reference report, the first volume in a new CDABI reference series. It examines digital asset regulatory frameworks across Europe, China, Hong Kong, Singapore, Russia, South Africa, East Africa, West Africa, and the Gulf. The 176-page report compares regulatory approaches to retail access, transaction monitoring, tax reporting, banking participation and central bank digital currencies. It also presents 13 policy findings and outlines six decisions Ghana could consider without introducing new legislation. The report draws on 313 sources and reflects legal and market developments as of September 30, 2026. Dr Afaglo said Ghana enacted its virtual asset law, Act 1154, in December 2025, with the Bank of Ghana Virtual Assets Department (VAD) supervising the sector. He said decisions on regulating digital assets would determine whether Ghana became an active participant in emerging payment systems or remained an endpoint. He said the report provided regulators, banks, and industry players with a common evidence base for considering policy options. “Rules for a New Money”, authored by Dr Afaglo and published by Vessel & Light Publishing, describes how Ghana’s virtual asset regulatory framework developed. The book examines the policy trade-offs, discussions between regulators and industry players, and outstanding decisions concerning the sector’s regulation. Dr Afaglo said the book documented the reasoning behind Ghana’s regulatory choices, which he said the final regulations would not necessarily explain. He said Cape Town was an appropriate venue for the main launch because South Africa had developed a regulatory framework for crypto assets that other African jurisdictions frequently studied. CDABI offers print copies of the reference report, while Vessel & Light Publishing offers “Rules for a New Money”. Amazon is expected to list paperback and Kindle editions of both books after the Cape Town launch.

items.title: Telecel Foundation equips 100 hearing-impaired students with practical STEM skills
items.description: The Telecel Foundation extended its commitment to inclusive learning to the Volta School for the Deaf in Hohoe, Volta Region, where 100 students took part in hands-on robotics training as part of Telecel Ghana’s Care Month celebrations. Facilitated by the Mingo Foundation, the workshop introduced students to practical STEM concepts through engaging activities designed to build creativity, teamwork and problem-solving skills. The initiative underscored a simple principle: every child, regardless of ability, deserves the opportunity to explore science, technology, engineering and mathematics and fulfil their potential. Speaking at the event, Rita Agyeiwaa Rockson, Foundation, Sustainability and External Communications Manager at Telecel Ghana, described the initiative as the Foundation’s way of creating meaningful impact during Care Month. “At Telecel, Care Month is dedicated to our customers and employees across Ghana. For the Foundation, we wanted to provide care that truly counts, which is why we are here today. Seeing these students grasp basic engineering concepts so quickly and build their projects with minimal guidance proves that ability should never define potential. Every child deserves the opportunity to become tomorrow’s engineer, innovator or problem-solver.” The school’s headmaster, Joe Innocent Kodjo Tsameny, thanked the Telecel Foundation for the robotics training. “Opportunities like this help bring out the potential in our students. As the world becomes increasingly digital, I am pleased they are gaining practical, hands-on robotics experience. This training has enabled them to apply the concepts they have learned in theory. He said. Telecel employee volunteers worked alongside the students throughout the day, offering guidance and encouragement as they completed their projects. One of the day’s standout participants was 13-year-old Makafui, the first among her peers to complete her project. Speaking through a sign language interpreter, she shared that the experience had inspired her to dream bigger. “I was very happy to finish first. The facilitators helped us understand each step, and I really enjoyed building my project. This training has inspired me to pursue a career in STEM. Thank you, Telecel Foundation, for giving us this opportunity.” Through initiatives like this, the Telecel Foundation continues to expand access to quality learning opportunities, equipping more young people with the confidence, skills, and inspiration to help shape the future through STEM.

items.title: Obuasi SHTS abuse allegations: WILI demands independent probe, protection for students
items.description: Women in Leadership International (WILI) has called for a thorough, independent investigation into allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School. The organisation also wants immediate protection and support for affected students, amid reports that some complaints may not have received timely attention. In a statement, WILI expressed concern about the alleged abuse and questions surrounding how the complaints were handled. “Schools must be places of learning, safety and opportunity, not environments where children fear exploitation, intimidation or abuse by those entrusted with their care,” it said. WILI acknowledged steps taken by the Ghana Education Service and other relevant authorities to investigate. However, it said the seriousness of the allegations required an impartial and transparent process. The investigation, it said, must establish the facts, examine possible institutional failures and ensure accountability wherever wrongdoing is established. The organisation also raised concerns about reports that some affected students and families may have faced pressure or intimidation. “No girl should be afraid to report abuse. No parent should fear consequences for seeking justice for their child. And no position of authority should place anyone beyond scrutiny,” the statement said. WILI urged investigators to examine all credible allegations, including any failures to report, prevent or respond appropriately to suspected abuse. It called for confidential counselling, protection from intimidation and access to appropriate medical and legal assistance for affected students. The organisation stressed that the investigation and any related disruptions must not undermine the girls’ education or future opportunities. It also urged authorities to strengthen safeguarding systems in schools through accessible reporting channels, clear professional boundaries, mandatory reporting procedures and effective accountability mechanisms. WILI requested regular public updates on the investigation, while protecting the privacy, dignity and safety of students and preserving the integrity of the process. The organisation acknowledged the right of every accused person to due process and the presumption of innocence. It said these principles must coexist with the duty to protect children and investigate complaints promptly. It appealed to government institutions, school authorities, parents, civil society organisations and communities to work together to make schools safer for girls. “A girl’s education should open doors to her future, not expose her to harm,” the statement said. “Protecting our girls is not optional. It is a collective responsibility.”

items.title: Upper East specialists seek urgent equipment boost as GMTF eases cancer care costs
items.description: Medical specialists in the Upper East Region have called for the swift delivery of diagnostic equipment to complement the financial relief provided by the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF). They say the Fund is helping patients afford specialised treatment, but better-equipped facilities are essential for early diagnosis and effective care, particularly for breast cancer. The appeal came during an engagement with GMTF management, led by Administrator Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, as part of its nationwide stakeholder consultations. The Medical Director of the Upper East Regional Hospital, Dr Joseph Kojo Tambil, commended the Fund for supporting several patients at the facility. He said the assistance relieved families who would otherwise struggle to pay for treatment. Expanding that support, he added, would help more patients with chronic conditions access specialised care. However, Dr Tambil urged the Fund to expedite the delivery of equipment promised to the hospital, particularly for breast cancer diagnosis. He said the equipment would strengthen diagnostic services, support early detection and improve treatment outcomes. A surgeon at the hospital, Dr Victor Dassa, highlighted the emotional and financial burden cancer places on patients and their families. He said treatment costs could severely strain household finances and prevent some patients from getting the care they need. Dr Dassa described the Fund as an important intervention for families facing these difficulties and stressed the need for sustained support. In response, Ms Darko-Opoku acknowledged the additional challenges patients face when they must travel long distances for specialised services. She said transport costs could compound the difficulties families already face in financing treatment. The Administrator explained that the Fund’s mandate extended beyond financial assistance. Access to quality care also depended on appropriate infrastructure, diagnostic equipment and specialised services. She stressed the importance of strengthening facilities in underserved communities to ensure that financial support translated into better patient care. The consultations aim to identify gaps in specialised healthcare, strengthen partnerships with medical professionals, and tailor the Fund’s interventions to patients’ and health facilities’ needs.

items.title: TOR slashes debt from $650m to $300m, MD reveals
items.description: The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) has reduced its debt burden from $650 million to about $300 million under a restructuring programme supported by the Energy Sector Levies Act (ESLA), Mr Edmond Kombat, Managing Director (MD) of TOR, has announced. Mr Kombat said it has also settled its exposures to four banks, and the debt reduction formed part of broader efforts to restore the financial viability of the state-owned refinery. Delivering a speech on the refinery’s turnaround during the Government Accountability Series Press Conference at the Presidency in Accra recounted that when the National Democratic Congress (NDC) government handed over to the New Patriotic Party (NPP) administration in January 2017, the TOR was operational. The refinery has processed about five million barrels of crude in 2016, with about two million barrels remaining in storage at the time of the handover. Mr Kombat noted that key infrastructure and equipment had been secured, including the offshore mooring facility, into which approximately $90 million in capital was injected in March 2017, as well as a new furnace and boiler to support continued operations. The Managing Director indicated that the restructuring and infrastructure investments were aimed at positioning TOR to operate more efficiently and sustainably, reducing its reliance on state support while strengthening its contribution to Ghana’s downstream petroleum sector. He said the Refinery had also shown that Ghana could refine its own crude, stating that in December 2016, TOR received its first delivery of Ghanaian indigenous crude from the TEN field for domestic refining aboard MT Bodeira. He noted that by the time the current Management took office in 2025, TOR’s position had deteriorated. “The Company had accumulated losses of about GH¢10 billion, and its debt had risen from $300 million in 2016 to about US$517 million,” Mr Kombat said. He noted that the Crude Distillation Unit (CDU) had been out of operation since April 2021; while the Residue Fluid Catalytic Cracking (RFCC) Unit had been shut down since 2019. He said these major units had not received the required maintenance, and TOR had been reduced largely to renting out storage space to petroleum service providers, instead of carrying out its core mandate. Mr Kombat reiterated that they met a Refinery that was not refining and a tank farm used only for limited storage. He said much of the infrastructure was run down or obsolete, and 18 out of the refinery’s 59 storage tanks were out of service and that some of the storage tanks had been out of service since 2004. Mr Kombat said TOR had not filed audited financial statements for six consecutive years, 2019 to 2024; saying, “for six years, the Refinery had no Audited Accounts”. He said the Company owed GH¢200 million to the Ghana Revenue Authority and GH¢20 million to the SSNIT, in addition to amounts owed to the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) and the Ghana Water Company as well as GH¢190 million in outstanding obligations to staff provident fund, retirees and resignees. The MD said TOR was several years delinquent in statutory payments. He said staff morale was low, staff were leaving, the workforce was divided, and more than 300 petitions over delayed promotions, some dating back to 10 years were awaiting review. Mr Kombat said the Refinery also owed other commercial entities and state-owned companies including Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) and the Volta River Authority (VRA). “The refinery was on the verge of being sold or leased for $21m. By the end of 2024, TOR had negative equity of GH¢7.6billion,” the MD said. Mr Kombat noted that between 2019 to 2024, TOR sold third party products belonging to three petroleum services providers, valued at millions of dollars to pay staff salaries without the knowledge of the product owners. Touching on what had changed since May 2025, Mr Kombat said since May 2025, under President John Dramani Mahama’s Reset Agenda, Management of TOR had taken steps to rebuild the company from within, beginning with people and stronger cash controls. He said they reviewed the outstanding promotion petitions and addressed eligible cases and that they also extended the operating hours at the refinery’s loading gantry, improved cash controls and accountability in product handling, worked to restore confidence and won back private petroleum companies and regional partners to store and lift products at TOR. Mr Kombat said these measures formed part of Project Restore TOR, a broader recovery programme to return the refinery into operations, improve its financial position and prepare it for long-term sustainability. He reiterated that Management made the rehabilitation and restart of the Crude Distillation Unit (CDU) its immediate operational priority. He said a Turnaround Maintenance Committee was constituted, and the work was funded solely from TOR’s IGF and carried out by TOR’s engineers and technicians. This, he said, was necessary to address years of deferred maintenance and prepare the plant for safe and reliable operations.

items.title: ‘Ghana was very high risk, but we were fortunate’ – Prof Amuasi on 2014–15 Ebola outbreak
items.description: Ghana faced a very high risk of Ebola during the 2014–15 West African outbreak, despite recording no cases, Global Health Leader at the KCCR, Prof John Amuasi, has said. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, he described Ghana’s escape as fortunate. He also questioned whether airport temperature checks can detect infected travellers. “Ghana was very high risk, but we were fortunate we did not get any cases,” he told host Kofi Agyei. His comments followed a question about whether Ghana’s lack of recorded cases reflected inadequate screening during the outbreak. Prof Amuasi explained that screening identifies people with possible symptoms. Testing must then establish whether they have the disease. He said headaches, fever and a generally sick appearance were not specific to Ebola. Detecting those symptoms alone could not confirm an infection. The regional experience showed how quickly the disease could cross borders. Nigeria’s outbreak began in July 2014, after an infected traveller arrived from Liberia. It recorded 20 cases and eight deaths. Senegal recorded one confirmed case and no deaths. Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone bore the greatest burden. The wider epidemic continued into 2016, with 28,610 reported cases and 11,308 deaths across those three countries, according to the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention . For Prof Amuasi, monitoring travellers after arrival deserves greater attention. “The key is keeping tabs on every single person who is coming in,” he said. He suggested that authorities could consider mandatory check-ins for basic signs and symptoms every two to three days. “I mean, it’s going to be a bit painful, but maybe that’s a more efficient thing, better thing to do.” He ruled out testing every arriving passenger. “But certainly, we cannot introduce mass testing for Ebola for every single person there who lands. That’s not practicable.” At the time of the interview, he said Ghana had no confirmed or suspected case. He therefore stressed public awareness, particularly among people entering the country. “And right now, given that there is no confirmed or even suspected case in the country, there is really nothing more to do than make people aware.”

items.title: Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani posted to Pindi bench after reshuffle at Lahore High Court
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani has returned to the twin cities following a reshuffle at the Lahore High Court (LHC), according to the court’s duty roster for November and December 2026. He will preside over a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry. Justice Kayani hails from Islamabad, while Islamabad and Rawalpindi are traditionally referred to as the twin cities. He was transferred to the LHC in April this year and assigned to its principal seat in Lahore. Despite being a senior judge of the LHC, he was not assigned to any division bench. According to the new duty roster, three division benches at the LHC’s Rawalpindi registry will comprise Justice Sadaqat Ali Khan and Justice Syed Farhad Ali Shah, who will handle criminal matters; Justice Mirza Viqas Rauf and Justice Muhammad Raza Qureshi, who will handle civil matters; and a special division bench comprising Justice Mirza Viqas Rauf and Justice Syed Farhad Ali Shah. The six single benches at the Rawalpindi registry will be headed by Justices Sadaqat Ali Khan, Mirza Viqas Rauf, Mohsin Akhtar Kayani, Muha­mmad Raza Qureshi, Malik Javid Iqbal Wains and Syed Farhad Ali Shah. The roster will remain in effect from Nov 2 to Dec 24, 2026. Justice Kayani previously served as the senior puisne judge of the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and was expecting to be elevated to chief justice. However, the transfer of Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar from the LHC, along with two other judges from the Sindh and Balochistan high courts, prompted him to challenge the inter-high court transfers. The Supreme Court’s constitutional bench upheld the transfers to the IHC, including that of Justice Dogar, who is now its chief justice. The decision, however, triggered a broader legal battle. Justice Kayani and other senior IHC judges approached the SC to challenge the administrative powers exercised by Chief Justice Dogar. They alleged that the office had been turned into a “monocracy” and that judges could be excluded from the roster at will. Following his own transfer to the LHC, Justice Kayani lost his seniority and was placed 12th on the high court’s seniority list. The new duty roster assigns him only to a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry, despite his previous position as the IHC’s senior puisne judge and his pending challenge to the inter-high court transfers. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

items.title: Cisjordanie : une commission de l’ONU accuse Israël de crimes contre l’humanité
items.description: Une commission d’enquête internationale mandatée par les Nations unies accuse les autorités et les forces israéliennes d’avoir commis des crimes contre l’humanité en Cisjordanie, notamment des actes d’extermination, de torture, de viol et de persécution. Israël rejette fermement ces conclusions, tandis que le rapport fait état d’une forte aggravation des violences depuis octobre 2023. Une nouvelle accusation visant Israël sur le terrain du droit international. Lundi 26 octobre, une commission d’enquête internationale mandatée par l’ONU a accusé les autorités et les forces israéliennes d’avoir commis des crimes contre l’humanité à l’encontre des Palestiniens en Cisjordanie occupée. Dans son rapport, elle cite notamment l’extermination, la torture, le viol et d’autres formes de violences sexuelles, ainsi que la persécution fondée sur des motifs discriminatoires liés notamment à la nationalité, à la race et à l’appartenance ethnique. La commission maintient également ses accusations de génocide concernant la bande de Gaza, déjà formulées dans un précédent rapport. Les autorités israéliennes rejettent ces accusations, qu’elles qualifient de mensongères et d’antisémites. Une dégradation marquée de la situation depuis octobre 2023 Dans son rapport, publié à la veille des élections législatives israéliennes, la commission estime que la situation en Cisjordanie s’est fortement détériorée depuis les attaques du Hamas du 7 octobre 2023, qui ont déclenché la guerre à Gaza. Selon les données citées par la commission, six Palestiniens avaient été tués par des frappes aériennes entre 2008 et le 6 octobre 2023. Entre le 7 octobre 2023 et le 30 septembre 2026, ce nombre est passé à 254. Le rapport décrit une combinaison d’opérations militaires israéliennes et de violences persistantes commises par des colons. La commission estime que les autorités israéliennes ont cherché à punir collectivement la population civile palestinienne en réaction aux attaques du 7 octobre. Elle dénonce ainsi ce qu’elle décrit comme une « attaque généralisée et systématique contre les civils », marquée par des morts, des blessures et des destructions de logements. Plus de 33 000 Palestiniens déplacés de force Les déplacements de population constituent un autre point central des préoccupations internationales. Le 4 septembre, le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme avait accusé Israël d’avoir déplacé de force plus de 33 000 Palestiniens de trois camps de réfugiés en Cisjordanie au début de l’année 2025. Il avait évoqué la possibilité de crimes contre l’humanité et de nettoyage ethnique. Israël occupe la Cisjordanie depuis 1967. Le territoire compte plus de trois millions de Palestiniens, ainsi qu’environ 500 000 Israéliens vivant dans des colonies considérées comme illégales au regard du droit international. La commission souligne également l’expansion de la colonisation, notamment à travers la multiplication des avant-postes, dans un contexte de tensions accrues entre Palestiniens, forces israéliennes et colons. Son président, Srinivasan Muralidhar, estime que les meurtres et les blessures intentionnellement infligés à des civils palestiniens, associés à la destruction de logements et à l’absence persistante de responsabilité, s’inscrivent dans une stratégie plus large visant à déplacer les Palestiniens et à leur imposer des conditions de vie insoutenables. La représentation israélienne auprès des Nations unies à Genève a immédiatement contesté les conclusions du rapport. Elle a dénoncé une campagne de désinformation visant, selon elle, à « diaboliser l’État d’Israël » et à présenter son existence comme criminelle. Ces accusations interviennent alors que la commission avait déjà conclu, dans un rapport publié en 2025, qu’Israël commettait un génocide à Gaza. Les autorités israéliennes avaient également rejeté cette conclusion. Le rapport aborde aussi la situation dans la bande de Gaza. Selon les chiffres du ministère de la Santé de Gaza, placé sous l’autorité du Hamas et dont les données sont considérées comme fiables par l’ONU, plus de 1 500 Palestiniens ont été tués depuis l’entrée en vigueur de la trêve en octobre 2025. La commission dénonce notamment les risques encourus par les civils qui s’approchent de la « ligne jaune », délimitant la zone sous contrôle des forces israéliennes, ou la franchissent. The post Cisjordanie : une commission de l’ONU accuse Israël de crimes contre l’humanité appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Makkah pact allies move from defence to diplomacy
items.description: • Pakistan’s army chief, Saudi defence minister, Turkish spymaster meet top Iranian officials • Pezeshkian backs understanding ‘to strengthen unity among Muslim nations’ • Saudis say visit aimed at supporting Qatari, Pakistani mediation efforts • Halting Houthi attacks, reopening Hormuz among main concerns ISLAMABAD: Iran on Monday expressed support for efforts to promote security and development as President Masoud Pezeshkian met senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the three signatories to the Makkah defence pact, with both sides agreeing to continue dialogue on regional peace and security. “The Islamic Republic of Iran supports any understanding aimed at strengthening the unity and cohesion of Islamic nations,” President Pezeshkian was quoted as saying in an official statement. He added that regional countries could set an example of justice and development by pooling their resources and capabilities. The meeting brought together Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Iran was represented by senior officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. The visiting officials met with Mr Rezaei separately ahead of their meeting with President Pezeshkian. During the preliminary meeting, it was decided that they would “continue their dialogue to bolster cooperation among the four regional nations, including in the areas of regional peace and security.” The talks followed Field Marshal Munir’s visit to Tehran last week, where he had proposed the meeting, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. The first meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries with Tehran reflected the realisation that regional tensions need to be addressed through diplomacy, even as the participating countries strengthen their own defence cooperation. (RIGHT) Iranian National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei, President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during talks between Makkah pact members and Iran in Tehran.—AFP Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry described the visit as part of continuing efforts by the agreement’s members to reduce tensions, promote dialogue and support diplomatic solutions. The visit, it said, was aimed to support the mediation efforts of Qatar and Pakistan. Abdul Aziz Hamad Al-Uwaisheq, assistant secretary-general for political affairs and negotiations at the Gulf Cooperation Council, similarly identified de-escalation, dialogue and support for Pakistan and Qatar led mediation as key objectives of the initiative. A Qatari delegation had immediately preceded the visit by Makkah pact officials to Tehran, suggesting coordination between the diplomatic initiatives. The discussions took place against a backdrop of heightened concern over the escalating conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah rebels against Saudi Arabia, the security of the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran. Moreover, the meeting coincided with Egyptian parliament authorising its president to provide defensive military support to Saudi Arabia in its conflict with Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement. Cairo has, meanwhile, maintained contacts with Iran, the United States and other regional partners in an effort to prevent the conflict from widening. In a way the meeting was also an extension of the R4 initiative, with Cairo conducting its diplomacy with Tehran in parallel and the other three going over to Tehran to see Iranian leaders. Iran has long argued that regional security should be managed by countries in the region rather than outside powers. Monday’s meeting offered Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye an opportunity to convey their concerns directly to Iranian leaders, while exploring whether regional cooperation could help contain the risks of a wider conflict. Media reports said the discussions included the possibility of a regional non-aggression framework, along with the resumption of US-Iran negotiations, halting Ansar Allah attacks, the reopening of Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. Other issues reportedly raised included the consequences of US and Israeli military actions and developments in Palestine and Lebanon. There was no immediate indication that the participants had reached an agreement on these issues after their meeting that lasted about two hours. Mr Rezaei, however, speaking to the media later, said, “a new and positive atmosphere has emerged within the region as reflected in the dialogues held with senior officials from Turkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia.” For Pakistan, the initiative offers a means of maintaining its defence partnership with Saudi Arabia while keeping channels open with neighbouring Iran. Islamabad has also sought to facilitate communication between Washington and Tehran, an effort that would become more difficult if regional hostilities resumed. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces the task of strengthening protection for its territory and critical infrastructure from Houthi attacks and fallout of US/Israel-Iran conflict. Its participation in the talks suggests that closer defence cooperation with Pakistan and Turkiye is not precluding engagement with Tehran. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

items.title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
items.description: The allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle have put his daughter Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, under an uncomfortable spotlight. She has been dealing with this potential news time bomb out of sight for seven years, while sharing so much about her life in TV series and interviews. Thomas Markle has strongly rejected the claims as “lies” used to destroy his reputation. But could this complicated story prove to be a turning point for Meghan, who has had a complicated and often hostile relationship with the UK public? What has emerged so far calls into question some of the criticism she’s faced. Thomas Markle has strongly denied the allegations against him Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her. Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example. “She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William,” wrote one commentator in 2020. “Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it’s too late,” she was told on social media about her father. All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light. By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle in a letter from her father’s first wife, Roslyn Loveless. She says that is why she kept her distance and didn’t bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family. The police shared that letter with Meghan when she was classified as a working royal. It’s not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her. According to the Sussexes’ spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was underway, presumably while she was on official trips and had to put on a brave face. There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg. “I don’t want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too,” Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time. There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes. But that whole episode looks different in hindsight. That letter was far more fraught. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father. We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren. Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are “sick lies” which are trying to destroy his reputation. His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are “fake news” and “clickbait”. “There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there,” she wrote on X on Sunday. Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle. Thomas Markle in a photo with his daughter Meghan When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile. Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background. Meghan’s supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix. But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan. On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she’ll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else’s. It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters. A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her. That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always. For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn’t always translated well. But perhaps this complex, still developing story – and the light it sheds on previous years – might mean there’s a more rounded view of her in the future.

items.title: Rate hike divides business community
items.description: KARACHI: Foreign investors welcomed the State Bank of Pakistan’s (SBP) 50bps rate hike to 12 per cent on Monday, but the business community called it counterproductive for stabilisation, industrial growth and export competitiveness. M. Abdul Aleem, Secretary General of the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry, acknowledged the SBP’s move, saying it was needed to contain inflationary pressure and safeguard macroeconomic stability amid global energy price risks. However, with large-scale manufacturing growth recovering to 1.9pc in July-August FY26 and private-sector credit expanding 14.1pc year-on-year, it is equally important to sustain the emerging momentum in investment and economic activity, he said. As inflationary pressures are significantly influenced by external energy prices and domestic supply constraints, he emphasised that monetary tightening must be complemented by targeted supply-side reforms, fiscal discipline, competitive energy tariffs, broader tax-base coverage and predictable taxation and regulatory policies. Foreign investors back SBP’s move to curb inflation, while industry says it will hurt exports and growth In contrast, FPCCI President Atif Ikram Sheikh said raising the policy rate to an uncompetitive 12pc would further inflate borrowing costs for manufacturers already grappling with unprecedented high overheads, soaring utility tariffs and liquidity constraints. Instead of curbing inflation — driven largely by supply-side bottlenecks, energy costs and fiscal anomalies rather than excess demand — tight monetary policy has crippled domestic manufacturing, he said, urging the government and the State Bank to recalibrate the framework and bring the policy rate to single digits to make credit affordable for trade, SMEs and large-scale manufacturing. High interest rates also place an unmanageable debt-servicing burden on the exchequer and private borrowers, creating a cycle of fiscal distress and stagnant output, he said, asking the SBP to align rates with regional benchmarks. KCCI President Talat Mahmood warned that the hike would further raise the cost of doing business, discourage private-sector investment and undermine growth. He said Pakistan needs to strengthen its productive capacity, attract investment, generate employment and accelerate export-led growth but the policy rate hike will send the wrong signal to businesses planning to invest and expand. SITE Association of Industry President Abdul Hadi said the move would further aggravate industry problems at a time when factories are operating far below capacity and barely surviving. The business community has long demanded a single-digit policy rate, but industry’s real problems have again been ignored, he said, adding that high rates will not only make fresh funding harder but also increase the burden on existing loans. He said the rate hike would burden manufacturers, forcing formal businesses to shut down or scale back, as costlier borrowing would hit new investment, expansion and production. Korangi Association of Trade & Industry President Sheikh Umer Rehan said the hike could hurt industry, business growth, and recovery, adding that inflation could also be curbed by cutting energy costs, fixing taxation, improving the business climate, and implementing effective industrial policies. Pakistan Textile Exporters Association Chairman Rehan Naseem Bharara said the rate hike would raise working-capital costs, constrain investment and weaken global competitiveness at a time when industry is already grappling with expensive energy and financing. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026
